ety: From Middle English dabben (“to strike”), probably of North Germanic origin, related to Old Icelandic dabba (“to tap, slap”), perhaps ultimately imitative. s.def: In the Arabic script, the vowel point for u, appearing as a small curl placed above a letter ( ـُ ) and designating a short u /u/. If the Arabic letter و (wāw) immediately follows, it indicates a long ū /uː/.

ety: From Middle English date, from Old French date, datil, datille, from Latin dactylus (likely via Old Provençal datil), from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”) (from the resemblance of the date to a human finger), probably a folk-etymological alteration of a word from a Semitic source such as Arabic دَقَل (daqal, “variety of date palm”) or Hebrew דֶּקֶל (deqel, “date palm”). ety: From Middle English daub (noun), from Middle English dauben (“to plaster or whitewash; cover with clay; bespatter”, verb), from Old Northern French dauber (“to whitewash; plaster”), of uncertain origin. ex: My dear friend, I feel better as soon as you come sit beside my sickbed!

s.def: An ironic way to start (often after my) addressing an inferior or someone one dislikes.
ex: My dear man, you ought to think twice about who you're trying to blackmail.

ety: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535). Cognate with Old Saxon diuriða (“glory, honour; preciousness”), West Frisian djoerte (“love, dearness, value, worth”), Du…

Scarcity; a lack or short supply.

The dearth of A.I. chips has been exacerbated because Nvidia, a longtime provider of the chips, has a virtual lock on the market.

To cause or produce a scarcity in something.

s.def: The cessation of life and all associated processes; the end of an organism's existence as an entity independent from its environment and its return to an inert, non-living state.
ex: My grandfather died/met a violent death, which saddened the whole family.

ety: From death + penalty.

ex: Joe Biden deserves the death penalty and Jonald Trump bad.

s.def: A decree that someone be put to death as a punishment for a crime; a sentence of execution.
ex: Comrades, here and now I pronounce the death sentence upon Snowball.

ex: To the confusion and confounding of that cursed death's-head knight.
This Komarov, a Cossack’s son, was a very short man with a crew cut and a death's-head's nostrils.

ety: From Middle English dethbed, from Old English dēaþbedd (“deathbed; grave”), equivalent to death + bed. Cognate with Swedish dödsbädd (“deathbed”). Compare also Dutch sterfbed (“deathbed”), German Sterbebett and Totenbett (both “deathbed”), Danish dødsleje (“deathbed”).

ex: He was once on his way to an old woman, who was on her death-bed and who had led a wicked life.

ety: From French débâcle, from débâcler (“to unbar; unleash”) from prefix dé- (“un-”) + bâcler (“to dash, bind, bar, block”) [perhaps from unattested Middle French and Old French *bâcler, *bacler (“to hold in place, prop a door or window open”)], from Vulgar Latin *bacculare, from Latin baculum (“rod, staff used for support”), from Proto-Indo-European *bak-. ety: From Anglo-Norman debarrer.

ex: As for the guides, they were debarred from the pleasure of discourse, the one being placed in the van, and the other obliged to bring up the rear.

ex: How can I then return in happy plight, That am debarr'd the benefit of rest?

ety: From French débarquer, from de- (Old French des-) + barque (“bark, small ship”).

ety: From de- + base, from Old French bas, from Latin bassus. Cognate with Spanish debajo (“under, beneath, below”). Compare abase.

ety: From Old French debatable (French débattable), equivalent to debate + -able.

ex: Just how many glaucoma patients there are in the United States and just how prevalent is the disease are two unknowns or at least two debatables.

ety: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic desbattere, from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (“to beat, to fence”).

a wise council […] that did debate this business

ex: The debate over the age of the universe is thousands of years old.

ex: There has been considerable debate concerning exactly how to format these articles.

Strife, discord.

s.def: The ousting or destruction of the ruling body of a government or other organization.
ex: A decapitation strike carried out by drone killed many of the country's senior generals.
Even those who welcome the decapitation of the Iranian regime may feel deep unease about America’s behavior.

s.def: The unseating of a senior politician.
ex: The decapitation of the Foreign Secretary was a significant publicity coup for the opposition.
The Lib Dem contender hoping to accomplish a bit of pre-emptive decapitation is Andrew Crawford.
Some also thought that the Lib Dem decapitation strategy had kept him cornered in his constituency during the campaign, unable to play a wider role.

Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English carbonize English decarbonize From de- + car…

s.def: To remove carbon from something.
ex: During the overhaul, the cylinder heads were found to be reusable, as long as they got a good cleaning to decarbonize the valve seat areas.

ety: From dec- + are.

s.def: A unit of surface area equal to 10 ares (that is, 1,000 square metres, 0.10 hectares, or approximately 0.25 acres)

ety: From dec- + athlete.

s.def: An athlete who competes in the decathlon.

ety: From dec- + -athlon, coined for the 1912 Summer Olympics in analogy to the word pentathlon.

s.def: An athletic contest consisting of ten events which includes sprinting, hurdling, jumping, and throwing over a span of two days.
ex: He entered U.C.L.A. in 1954 and played for the renowned coach John Wooden’s basketball team there while training for decathlons.
For now, Gray and her peers are able to compete for Olympic berths only in the seven-event heptathlon, while the decathlon is restricted to men.

s.def: A contest in science and math proving skill.

ety: From Middle English decaien (“to decrease, diminish”) and decai (“deterioration, decline in value”), from Anglo-Norman decaeir (“to fall away, decay, decline”), from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, etymologically restored form of Latin dēcidere (“to fall down, to fail, sink or perish”), from de- (“of, from, away, down”) + cadere (“to fall”). Compare decadent and decadence.

s.def: To deteriorate, to get worse, to lose strength or health, to decline in quality.
ex: The pair loved to take pictures in the decaying hospital on forty-third street.

s.def: Rot; any processes or result of organic matter being gradually decomposed, especially by microbial action.
ex: tooth decay/dental decay—wood-decay fungi—bacterial decay—photochemical decay

s.def: Deterioration of condition; loss of status, quality, strength, or fortune.
ex: civic and moral decay—systemic decay—fall into decay—urban decay—arrested decay—memory decay
Although the best room of the inn, it had the melancholy aspect of grandeur in decay, and was much too vast for comfort.

s.def: Radioactive decay; decomposition of an atom or its nucleus.
ex: alpha decay—gamma decay—fission decay—decay chain

s.def: Continuous decrease of a quantity.
ex: exponential decay—decay rate—orbital decay—decay time—decay constant—time decay

s.def: Overthrow, destruction, ruin, death.
Array decay.
Particle decay; decomposition of a sub-atomic particle.
To undergo optical decay, that is, to relax to a less excited state, usually by emitting a photon or phonon.
To change by undergoing fission, by emitting radiation, or by capturing or losing one or more electrons; to undergo radioactive decay.
ex: Uranium decays to radium through a long series of steps with a cumulative half-life of 4.4 billion years.

ety: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

s.def: Death, departure from life.
ex: So should that beauty which you hold in lease Find no determination: then you were Yourself again after yourself's decease […]

s.def: To die.
ex: After which usurped victorie, he presently deceased: and partly through the excessive joy he thereby conceived.

s.def: To cause to die.

ety: From Latin decedens, present active participle of decedere (“to depart, die”).

s.def: A dead person.
ex: “A check of the nightstands revealed large amounts of prescription medication in the decedent’s name,” the coroner’s notes said, according to TMZ.com.

s.def: Removing; departing; deceased.
ex: satisfy every claimant upon the estate of a decedent person

ety: From Middle English deceyte, from Old French deceite, deçoite, from decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin dēcipere (“to cheat, mislead”).

s.def: An act or practice intended to deceive; a trick.
ex: The whole conversation was merely a deceit.

s.def: An act of deceiving someone.
ex: Upon his return he killed Eriphyle for her vanity and deceit of him and his father.

s.def: The state of being deceitful or deceptive.

The tort or fraudulent representation of a material fact made with knowledge of its falsity, or recklessly, or without reasonable grounds for believing its truth and with intent to induce reliance on it; the plaintiff justifiably relies on the deception, to his injury.
A group of lapwings.
ex: Deceits of lapwings were preparing to migrate
These birds belonged to a deceit of lapwings that had been displaced from their tract of grasslands and marshy grounds by a housing development.

ety: From Middle English deceyven, from Anglo-Norman deceivre, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive; beguile; entrap”), from dē- (“from”) + capiō (“to seize”); see captive. Compare conceive, perceive, receive. Displaced native Old English beswīcan.

s.def: To trick or mislead.
ex: It feels painful to begin seeing clearly, that you’ve been deceived by the very people and institutions you trusted to guide you.

ety: Late 19th c., from de- + (ac)celerate. Compare deaccelerate.

s.def: To reduce the velocity of something.
To reduce the rate of advancement of something, such as a disease.
To go slower.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ Proto-Italic *dekəm Latin decem Latin December Latin decemberbor. Old French decembrebor. Middle English December English December From Middle English December, Decembre, from Old French decembre, from Latin december (“tenth month”), from Latin decem (“ten”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; December was the tenth month in the Roman calendar.

s.def: The twelfth and last month of the Gregorian calendar, following November and preceding the January of the following year, containing the southern solstice.
ex: Holonyms: calendar year; year
It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012.

s.def: A female given name transferred from the month name [in turn from English].
A surname.

ety: From December + -ist, a calque of Russian декабри́ст (dekabríst).

s.def: A participant in, or sympathizer with, the Decembrist revolt.

ety: From Latin decemvir.

s.def: Any of two groups of 10 men selected in 451 and 450 B.C. to wield complete power over Rome and establish the laws of the Twelve Tables.
Any member of a decemvirate, a council or ruling body of 10 people, as the Venetian Council of Ten.

ety: From Latin decentia, from decens. Equivalent to decent + -cy. Compare French décence.

s.def: The quality of being decent; propriety.
ex: Immodest words admit of no defence, / For want of decency is want of sense.
[To Joseph McCarthy:] Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?

s.def: That which is proper or becoming.
ex: Those thousand decencies, that daily flow / From all her words and actions.

ety: From Latin decennialis, from decennium (“10-year period”) + -ālis, from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (“-ium”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from decem (“ten”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives).

s.def: Synonym of decade, a ten-year period.
A tenth anniversary, particularly
Occurring every ten years.
Of or related to a ten-year period, as a term of office.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French décent, or its source, Latin decēns, present participle of decet (“it is fitting or suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to take, accept, to receive, greet, be suitable”) (compare Ancient Greek δοκέω (dokéō, “to appear, seem, think”), δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to accept”); Sanskrit दशस्यति (daśasyáti, “shows honor, is gracious”), दाशति (dāśati, “makes offerings, bestows”)). Meaning ‘kind, pleasant’ is from 1902.

s.def: Appropriate; suitable for the circumstances.
Having a suitable conformity to basic moral standards; showing integrity, fairness, or other characteristics associated with moral uprightness.
ex: Zohran Mamdani is a decent man for not accepting the pay rise he’s entitled to, as he wishes to see that money go to the poor of New York.

s.def: Sufficiently clothed or dressed to be seen.
ex: Are you decent? May I come in?

s.def: Fair; acceptable; okay.
ex: He's a decent saxophonist, but probably not good enough to make a career of it.

s.def: Significant; substantial.
ex: There are a decent number of references out there, if you can find them.

s.def: Conforming to perceived standards of good taste.
Comely; shapely; well-formed.
Misspelling of descent.

The state of being decentralized.

ex: decentralize operations

s.def: To reduce the authority of (a governing body) by distributing that authority among several bodies.
ex: decentralize authority
decentralize decision-making
The government planned to decentralize power to local councils.

s.def: To become decentralized.
To bring (a suspect) to the ground by use of directed force; to tackle.

ety: From Middle English decepcioun, from Old French decepcion, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

s.def: An instance of actions and/or schemes fabricated to mislead someone into believing a lie or inaccuracy.
ex: deliberate deception
pure deception
She got the money out of the tourist by deception.

ety: From Middle French déceptif, from Latin dēceptīvus, from dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

s.def: Likely or attempting to deceive.
ex: deceptive practices
Appearances can be deceptive.
[…] at the opening of the campaign, the French, after various deceptive attempts on different places, suddenly invested Tournay.

ety: From de- + cerebrate.

s.def: Having the cerebrum removed.
ex: In this respect the decerebrate condition offers some resemblance to the cataleptic state.
All brain tissue rostral to the diencephalon was removed, making the preparation a decerebrate one.

s.def: To remove the cerebrum in order to eliminate brain function.
ex: […] and the correct principles of delivering it through the different straits of the pelvis after the head has been decerebrated and crushed.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English certify English decertify From de- + certify.

s.def: To annul the certification of.
ex: Nigeria was tagged as a transit-route of drug carriers. This prompted the United States government to decertify the country.

s.def: To annul a labor union.

ety: Borrowed from French déciare, equivalent to deci- + are.

s.def: A measure of area, equivalent to one tenth of an are, or ten square metres.

ety: From deci- + bel.

s.def: A common measure of intensity ratio (e.g. for sound) that is one tenth of a bel on the logarithmic intensity scale. It is defined as dB = 10 log₁₀(P₁ / P₂), where P₁ and P₂ are the relative intensities.

ety: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).

s.def: To resolve (a contest, problem, dispute, etc.); to choose, determine, or settle.
ex: The election will be decided on foreign policies.
It was decided to meet here at midnight.
Her last-minute goal decided the game.

s.def: To make a judgment, especially after deliberation.
ex: You must decide between good and evil.
I have decided that it is healthier to walk to work.
Since this cowl released a flutter of moths and parted at the shoulder as he was getting into it, he decided that it must be his own.

s.def: To cause someone to come to a decision.
ex: Your admonition decided me against my intended course of action.
It decides me to look into the matter, for if it is worth anyone's while to take so much trouble, there must be something in it.

s.def: Of a Turing machine: to return a correct answer (for some yes-or-no problem) on every possible input.
ex: No Turing Machine can decide the halting problem.
First, the hierarchy theorems tell us that a Turing machine can decide more languages in EXPSPACE than it can in PSPACE.

s.def: To cut off; to separate.
ex: Our seat denies us traffic here; / The sea, too near, decides us from the rest.

s.def: simple past and past participle of decide
Determined; resolute.
ex: A woman of decided opinions

s.def: Clear; unmistakable, definite, unquestionable.
ex: It was a decided victory.
There was a decided ugliness to the patch of waste ground.
The visual indicators are a decided improvement, and have reduced the telephoning by the staff in the signalbox.

s.def: A voter etc. who has reached their decision.
ex: […] but that is a highly flawed procedure if the undecideds differ in major ways from the decideds.

ety: Etymology tree Latin dēcidō Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Italic *-wos Latin -uus Latin dēciduuslbor. English deciduous Learned borrowing from Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“to fall down or off”) + -uus.

s.def: Describing a part that falls off, or is shed, at a particular time or stage of development.
ex: In the Hippoidea there is generally the full series of 44 teeth, but the first premolar is often deciduous or wanting in the lower or in both jaws.

s.def: Of or pertaining to trees which lose their leaves in winter or the dry season.
ex: . Compare caducous.
a deciduous tree

s.def: Transitory, ephemeral, not lasting.

ety: From French décigramme. By surface analysis, deci- + gram.

s.def: An SI unit of mass equal to 10⁻¹ grams. Symbol: dg

ety: From deci- + liter.

s.def: US spelling of decilitre.

ety: From dec- (“ten”) + -illion. First attested in 1709 in a translation of Johann Sturm’s Mathesis juvenilis by George Vaux, translating Latin mille myriades octavorum numerorum.

s.def: 10³³.
10⁶⁰.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin, Medieval Latin decimalis, from Latin decimus, from decem (“ten”) + adjective suffix -alis.

s.def: The decimal system itself.
A number expressed in the base-ten system, (particularly) a fractional numeral written in this system.
ex: What is ⁷⁄₂₃ as a decimal?

s.def: A decimal place.
ex: Pi has a value of 3.142, to three decimals.

s.def: A decimal point.
Alternative spelling of dismil.
A numerical system of counting in tens.

ety: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth; to tithe”) (see, from -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from decimus (“tenth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). As a noun, via Latin decimatus (“tithing area; tithing rights”).

s.def: to severely reduce
To kill one-tenth of (a group), (historical, specifically) as a military punishment in the Roman army selected by lot, usually carried out by the surviving soldiers.
ex: Shall we decimate them? That sounds good, nice word. Remove one-tenth of the population!

s.def: To destroy or remove one-tenth of (something).
To devastate: to reduce or destroy significantly but not completely.
ex: [England] had decimated itself for a question which involved no principle, and led to no result.
Um, some sort of power overload. I'm afraid it decimated your breakfast.
They can be devastating to certain plants if left uncontrolled: a downy mildew of grapes decimated European vineyards during the nineteenth century.

s.def: To exact a tithe or other 10% tax.
To tithe: to pay a 10% tax.
To divide into tenths; to decimalize.
To reduce to one-tenth: to destroy or remove nine-tenths of (something).
ex: In this dramatic picture, the nation is literally decimated, and even the tenth which remains is subjected to a further destruction.
In the New World, European colonists initially enslaved Native Americans, decimating the indigenous populations to one-tenth of their original sizes.

s.def: To replace (a high-resolution model) with another of lower but acceptable quality. (Usually algorithmically)
ex: A decimate tool allows us to obtain a more coarse-grained view of the data over the full n-dimensional space.
However, many times it is more practical to decimate existing high-res models because of time, money or manpower issues.
Given this initial fine mesh, we smooth and decimate it to a desired mesh resolution.

s.def: A tithe or other 10% tax or payment.

ety: Borrowed from French décimètre. Equivalent to deci- + meter.

s.def: US spelling of decimetre.

ety: Borrowed from French décimètre. By surface analysis, deci- + metre.

s.def: An SI unit of length equal to 10⁻¹ metres. Symbol: dm
ex: Holonyms: metre < kilometre < megametre < gigametre < terametre < petametre
Meronyms: picometre < nanometre < micrometre < millimetre < centimetre

ety: As decypher, but not retaining the y from the Old French etyma of cipher (cyfre, cyffre); the i spelling tends to be preferred etymologically, being consistent with its cognates, the French déchiffrer and the Italian decifrare, and with their common ancestor, the Medieval Latin cifra, cifera, ciphra. By surface analysis, de- + cipher.

s.def: To convert a code or cipher to plain text.
To read text that is almost illegible or obscure.
To make sense of a complex situation.
To find a solution to a problem.
A decipherment; a decoding.

ety: Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

s.def: A choice or judgement.
ex: It is the decision of the court that movies are protected as free speech.
His life has always been filled with big decisions.
It's a tough decision, but I'll take vanilla.

s.def: The act of deciding.
Firmness of conviction.
ex: After agonizing deliberations, they finally proceeded with decision.

s.def: A result arrived at by the judges when there is no clear winner at the end of the contest.
ex: He has won twice by knockout, once by decision.

s.def: A win or a loss awarded to a pitcher.
To defeat an opponent by a decision of the judges, rather than by a knockout
The process of reaching a decision.

ety: From Middle French décisif, equivalent to decide + -ive.

s.def: Having the power or quality of deciding a question or controversy; putting an end to contest or controversy; final; conclusive.
ex: decisive vote
decisive battle

s.def: Decided; definite; incontrovertible.
ex: decisive victory
[F]abulous forces are there encountered and a decisive victory is won: […]

s.def: Marked by promptness and decision, resolute; without hesitation.
ex: decisive action
a decisive person
A noble instance of this attribute of the decisive character.

ety: From Middle English dekke, borrowed from Middle Dutch dec (“roof, covering”), from Middle Dutch decken, from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Formed the same: German Decke (“covering, blanket”). Doublet of thatch and thack.

s.def: The floorlike covering of the horizontal sections, or compartments, of a ship or boat. Small vessels have only one deck; larger ships have two or three decks.
ex: Holonyms: watercraft, vessel, vessel
to swab the deck

s.def: A pack or set of playing cards.
To knock (someone) to the floor, especially with a single punch.
ex: Wow, did you see her deck that guy who pinched her?

s.def: Any raised flat surface that can be walked on: a balcony; a porch; a raised patio; a flat rooftop.
A main aeroplane surface, especially of a biplane or multiplane.
A set of cards owned by each individual player and from which they draw when playing.
Ellipsis of slide deck: a set of slides for a presentation.
ex: Navigate to the location where your PowerPoint deck is stored and select it.

s.def: A heap or store.
Ellipsis of tape deck.
The multiset of graphs formed from a single graph by deleting a single vertex in all possible ways.

ety: From deck + hand.

s.def: A member of the crew of a merchant ship who performs manual labour.
A stagehand.
ex: Sometimes actors set props on the spikes, or sometimes a deckhand will do it, depending on the action of the play.

ety: From Middle French declamer, from Latin dēclāmō.

s.def: To recite, e.g., poetry, in a theatrical way; to speak for rhetorical display; to speak pompously, noisily, or theatrically; bemouth; to make an empty speech; to rehearse trite arguments in debate; to rant.
ex: Grenville seized the opportunity to declaim on the repeal of the stamp act.

s.def: To speak rhetorically; to make a formal speech or oration; specifically, to recite a speech, poem, etc., in public as a rhetorical exercise; to practice public speaking.
ex: The students declaim twice a week.

s.def: To object to something vociferously; to rail against in speech.
ex: Declaiming such practices, Baskaran writes: 'The flow of the film would not be affected in the least if song sequences were excised, wholly or partly'

s.def: To disclaim, disavow.
ex: He now declaimed having intended any thing disrespectful to the Senate in the expression he had used.
Unless these conditions are fulfilled we declaim responsibility.
Of course, a small minority has always declaimed any religious affiliation, and some agnostics have been prominent figures in American public life.

ety: From French déclamation, from Latin dēclāmātiō, dēclāmātiōnem, from dēclāmō, dēclāmāre; see declaim.

s.def: The act or art of declaiming; rhetorical delivery; loud speaking in public.
A set or harangue; declamatory discourse.
Pretentious rhetorical display, with more sound than sense.
ex: mere declamation

ety: Equivalent to declaim + -atory.

s.def: Having the quality of a declamation.
Pretentiously lofty in style; bombastic.
ex: Behind him an excitable Frenchman was holding forth in declamatory style to a group of astonished residents.

ety: From Middle English declaration, declaracion, declaracioun, from Old French declaration (French déclaration), from Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of Latin dēclārātiō.

s.def: A list of items for various legal purposes, e.g. customs declaration.

In common law, the formal document specifying plaintiff's cause of action, including the facts necessary to sustain a proper cause of action, and to advise the defendant of the grounds upon which he is being sued.
The specification of an object, such as a variable or function, establishing its existence but not necessarily describing its contents.
An emphatic or formal act of saying, telling or asserting something, by speech or writing; a decisive assertion or proclamation.
Specifically, a declaration of love.
ex: I went to Miss Mills's, fraught with a declaration.

s.def: The act or process of declaring.
The act, by the captain of a batting side, of declaring an innings closed.
A formal announcement by a country or other body with military capability that it is in a state of war with another such entity.
ex: Make no mistake, the sway of the railways' mandate in the middle of the 19th century was, in some quarters, a declaration of war on the old.

ety: Calque of Latin dēclārātiō voluntātis, directly and indirectly from calques of it.

s.def: A private outward manifestation of intention which is directly aimed at bringing about a legal effect.

ety: From Middle English declaren, from Old French declarer, from Latin dēclārō (“to make clear”), from dē- + clārus (“clear”).

s.def: to make a declaration
To make clear, explain, interpret.
To assert or announce formally, officially, explicitly, or emphatically.
ex: He declared him innocent.
declare bankruptcy
declare victory

s.def: To inform government customs or taxation officials of goods one is importing or of income, expenses, or other circumstances affecting one's taxes.
ex: The prosecution has introduced evidence, including canceled checks, to show that the judge failed to declare part of his income.

s.def: To show one's cards in order to score.
For a constituency in an election to officially announce the result
ex: Houghton and Sunderland South was the first constituency to declare in the 2015 general election.

s.def: The decision of the captain to let the bowling side bat in test cricket to save time without being all out.
ex: He declared at 689-7.

s.def: To explicitly establish the existence of (a variable, function, etc.) without necessarily describing its content.
ex: The counter "i" was declared as an integer.

s.def: To declare war.
ex: France declared on me, I'm finished!

s.def: To state that a thing shall happen or affirm a condition in the hopes of seeing it happen spiritually, in contrast to prayer which takes the form of a request.
ex: He prayed to God "please heal my sister", while she declared "I am healed in Jesus' name".

s.def: To make a formal pronouncement, or sign a legal document, that initiates a state of war between one nation and another, usually before hostilities begin.
To announce one's intention to fiercely combat or eradicate something.
ex: The governor declared war on poverty.

ety: From late Middle English declinson, from Middle French declinaison (Modern French: déclinaison), from Latin dēclīnātiō. Doublet of declination.

s.def: The product of that act; a list of declined forms.
ex: a page full of declensions

s.def: A way of categorizing nouns, pronouns, or adjectives according to the inflections they receive.
A falling off, decay or descent.
The act of declining a word; the act of listing the inflections of a noun, pronoun or adjective in order.

ety: From Middle English declinacioun, borrowed from Middle French declination, from Latin declinatio. Doublet of declension.

s.def: At a given point, the angle between magnetic north and true north.
At a given point, the angle between the line connecting this point with the geographical center of the earth and the equatorial plane.
A refusal.
ex: the queen's declination from marriage

s.def: The gradual decline in the overall fundamental frequency or pitch of speech over the course of an utterance, independent of local variations such as tones and pitch accents.
Declension.
The act or state of bending downward; inclination.
ex: declination of the head

s.def: The act or state of falling off or declining from excellence or perfection; deterioration; decay; decline.
ex: the declination of monarchy
Summer […] is not looked on as a time of declination or decay.

s.def: Deviation.
ex: this declination of atoms in their descent
November 2, 1690, Robert South, Sinners Inexcusable from Natural Religion Only every violation of and declination from the rules

ety: From Middle English declinen, and ultimately Latin declīnō (“to bend, turn aside, deflect, inflect, decline”, from dē- (“down”) + clīnō (“to bend, to incline”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean). The senses arrived from two separate pathways in Middle English: * The grammatical sense came from Old English declīnian, which was borrowed directly from the Latin etymon. * All senses except the grammatical sense were derived from those of Old French decliner. ex: It is far better to grasp the universe as it really is than to persist in delusion, however satisfying and reassuring.

ex: Hess, always a muddled man though not so doltish as Rosenberg, flew on his own to Britain under the delusion that he could arrange a peace settlement.

s.def: An adamant belief in a falsehood despite incontestable evidence.

ety: From delusion + -al.

ex: You're delusional if you think that plan will work.

ety: Borrowed from French de luxe (“of luxury”), from Latin luxus (“excess”).

s.def: Very fine in quality or luxurious.
ex: The band released a deluxe version of their LP, containing bonus tracks and with a personal message by all the members in the sleeve.

ety: From Middle English delven, from Old English delfan (“to dig, dig out, burrow, bury”), from Proto-Germanic *delbaną (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelbʰ- (“to dig”). ety: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”). By surface analysis, dem- + -agogue.

ex: It is true that America has a paranoid streak in its politics, and demagogues come along from time to time to feed on anger and resentment.

s.def: A leader of the people.

ety: Back-formation from demarcation.

ex: But these words didn't follow the precepts of the metric system, the official standard for demarcating the universe into manageable, studyable chunks.

ety: First recorded c.1752, from Spanish línea de demarcación and/or Portuguese linha de demarcação, the demarcation line laid down by the Pope on May 4, 1493, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal on a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. ex: Everyone who wanted to speak did so. It was democracy in its purest form.

Given up by the guardian or owner; abandoned, forsaken.
ex: There was a derelict ship on the island.

s.def: Of property: in a poor state due to abandonment or neglect; dilapidated, neglected.
Adrift, lost.
Property abandoned by its former guardian or owner; (countable) an item of such property.
An abandoned or forsaken person; an outcast, a waif.
A homeless or jobless person; a vagrant; also, a person who is (perceived as) negligent in their hygiene and personal affairs.
ex: As they hunt, the Archers and Duval find many derelicts and ne'er-do-wells in many parts of Paris.

s.def: A person who is negligent in performing a duty.

ex: Had I not so marv'lously done / My works, ye had not had such heinous sin, / Of so damning, derelicting nature; / But now ye have no excuse, no cover.

ety: From Latin dērelictiō (“neglect, abandonment”), from dērelinquō (“to neglect, abandon”), from dē- + re- + linquō (“to leave”).

ex: The new soldier did not clean his cabin and was scolded for dereliction and disobedience.
What he did was a terrible dereliction of duty.
[…] there on the table were the uncleared remains of Thursday's lunch, plain evidence of someone's dereliction.

s.def: The act of abandoning something, or the state of being abandoned.
ex: To this we must contend with prayer , with actual dereliction and seposition of all our other affairs

s.def: Land gained from the water by a change of water-line.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate; to turn”) (referring to turning the mouth to smile) or *wreyd- (“to carve; to scratch”)). cognates * Old French dérider (rare), derire

s.def: To laugh at or mock (someone or something) harshly; to ridicule, to scorn.
ex: Cicero beeing Augur, derideth the Auguries, and blames men for letting their actions relie vpon the voyce of a Crovve or a Davve.

s.def: To laugh in a harshly mocking manner.

ety: From Latin *dērīsibilis (compare Italian derisibile, “deridable”), from dērīsus + -ibilis (whence English -ible), a variant of -bilis (adjective-forming suffix that denotes the capacity or worth of being acted upon). Dērīsus is the perfect passive participle of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (intensifying prefix) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (originally “to rotate or turn”, then specifically…

s.def: Deserving derision (“treatment with disdain or contempt”).

ety: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

s.def: Act of treating with disdain.
ex: There was just a touch of derision in the Don's voice and Hagen flushed.

s.def: Something to be derided; a laughing stock.
ex: Miss Briggs was not formally dismissed, but her place as companion was a sinecure and a derision […]

ety: From the participle stem of Latin dērīdeō (“to deride”) + -ive.

s.def: Expressing or characterized by derision; mocking; ridiculing.
ex: The critic's review of the film was derisive.
Johnson shook his head, a derisive grin ticking the corners of his mouth.

s.def: Deserving or provoking derision or ridicule.
ex: The plot of the film was so derisive that the audience began to jeer.

ety: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

s.def: A leading or drawing off of water from a stream or source.
The act of receiving anything from a source; the act of procuring an effect from a cause, means, or condition, as profits from capital, conclusions or opinions from evidence.
The act of tracing origin or descent; an instance thereof (for example, an etymology).
ex: the derivation of a word from an Indo-European root

s.def: Forming a new word by changing the base of another word or by adding affixes to it.
The state or method of being derived; the relation of origin when established or asserted.
That from which a thing is derived.
That which is derived; a derivative; the result of a deduction.
The process of deriving one thing from another, especially in logic; a deduction.
The process of application of the derivative operator to a function, yielding another function called the derived function of the first.

An algebraic generalization of the derivative operator (from its natural setting in the ring of real-valued functions) to a general associative algebra over a field. Formally, (given an algebra A over a field K) a K-linear endomorphism that satisfies Leibnitz's Law.

ety: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

s.def: Obtained by derivation; not radical, original, or fundamental.
ex: a derivative conveyance
a derivative word

s.def: Imitative of the work of someone else.
ex: No, I really felt it was very derivative. To me it it looked like it was straight out of Diane Arbus, but it had none of the wit.

s.def: Referring to a work, such as a translation or adaptation, based on another work that may be subject to copyright restrictions.
Having a value that depends on an underlying asset of variable value.
Something derived.
A chemical derived from another.

One of the two fundamental objects of study in calculus (the other being integration), which quantifies the rate of change, tangency, and other qualities arising from the local behavior of a function.
ex: The derivative of x² is 2x; if f(x)#61;x², then f'(x)#61;2x

s.def: A word formed by derivation, such as stylish from style.
A financial instrument whose value depends on the valuation of an underlying asset; such as a warrant, an option etc.

ety: From Middle English deriven, from Old French deriver, from Latin dērīvō (“to lead, turn, or draw off (a liquid), draw off, derive”), from dē (“away”) + rīvus (“a stream”); see rival. Unrelated to arrive.

s.def: To obtain or receive (something) from something else.
ex: Reading books is the best way to derive knowledge.
Bob the aforesaid, and his present chances of deriving a competent independence from the honourable profession to which he had devoted himself.

s.def: To deduce (a conclusion) by reasoning.
To find the derivation of (a word or phrase).
To originate or stem (from).
ex: Her excellent organisation skills derive from her time as a secretary in the army.
Britannia's firebox would appear to have derived from those of the Bulleid Pacifics, which it closely resembles.

s.def: To create (a compound) from another by means of a reaction.
To turn the course of (water, etc.); to divert and distribute into subordinate channels.
ex: For fear it [water] choke up the pits […] they [the workman] deriue it by other drains.

s.def: To differentiate (a function).
Of a function, another function, the value of which for any value of the independent variable is the instantaneous rate of change of the given function at that value of the independent variable.

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin derma, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”). Doublet of derm.

s.def: The inner layer of the skin.
Clipping of dermatologist.
A Jewish dish of roast or boiled seasoned meat and flour etc. in a casing, especially kishke.

s.def: Inflammation of the skin.

ety: From dermatology + -ist or dermato- + -logist.

s.def: A person who is skilled in, professes or practices dermatology.

ety: From Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”) + -logy. Analysable as dermato- + -logy.

s.def: The study of the skin and its diseases.

ety: From dermato- (“skin”) + -phyte (“plant”).

s.def: Any parasitic fungus (mycosis) that infects the skin (tinea, ringworm, jock itch, athlete's foot).

ety: From dermato- + -plasty.

s.def: Plastic surgery of the skin, especially the use of skin grafts.

ety: From dermato- + -osis.

s.def: Any disease of the skin.

ety: Borrowed from French dernier, a contraction of derrenier, from Old French derrain (“final, last”) (by analogy with premier), from Vulgar Latin *dēretrānus, from Latin dē (“from, away from”) + retrō (“back; backwards; behind”) + -ānus (“of or pertaining to”).

s.def: Final, last.

ety: Inherited from Late Middle English derogaten, from derogat(e) (“annulled, abrogated”, used participially and later as the past participle of derogaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix) borrowed from Latin dērogātus, perfect passive participle of dērogō (“to annul, repeal part of a law, take away, detract from”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dē- (“from”) + rogō (“to ask, enquire; to propose a law”). Sporadic participial usage of the adjective up until Earl…

s.def: To partially repeal (a law etc.).

s.def: To detract from (something); to disparage, belittle.
ex: When the need for self-affirmation is satisfied through other means, one is less compelled to derogate members of negatively stereotyped groups.

s.def: To take away (something from something else) in a way which leaves it lessened.
ex: Anything […] that should derogate, minish, or hurt his glory and his name.
It derogates little from his fortitude, while it adds infinitely to the honor of his humanity.

s.def: To detract from (a quality of excellence, authority etc.).
ex: In doing so she had derogated from her dignity and committed herself.

s.def: To act in a manner below oneself; to debase oneself.

Would Charles X. derogate from his ancestors? Would he be the degenerate scion of that royal line?

s.def: Derogated, annulled in part.
Debased, deteriorated.

ety: From Old French derogacion (French dérogation), from Latin dērogātiō.

s.def: An act which belittles; disparagement.
The act of derogating; the temporary or partial nullification of a law.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin dērogātōrius, from Latin dērogō; corresponding to derogate + -ory.

s.def: tending to lessen the value of
Disparaging.
Tending to derogate
Tending to derogate:
ex: Acts of Parliament derogatory from the power of subsequent Parliaments bind not.

s.def: Being or pertaining to a derogatory clause.
A tradeline on a credit report that indicates negative credit history.

ety: Named after British executioner Thomas Derrick, who invented the framework arrangement commonly known by this name to aid in the conduct of executions. First use appears c. 1600 in the publication Ballad Death Earl Essex.

To hoist with, or as if with, a derrick.
To remove (a pitcher).

ety: Named after American gunsmith Henry Deringer (1786–1868).

s.def: A type of very small, concealable pistol with one or two barrels but without any loading system or magazine.

ety: From de- + Russification or deruss(ify) + -ification.

ety: From Ottoman Turkish درویش (derviş), from Persian درویش (darvêš, “poor; Sufi mystic”), from Middle Persian dlgwš (driyōš, “poor, needy”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *drigu-, cognate with Sanskrit ध्रिगु (dhrigu, “needy”) and Avestan 𐬛𐬭𐬌𐬔𐬎 (driguš).

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English descenden (“to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to go from a better to a worse condition, decline, degenerate; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.”), from Anglo-Norman descendere, descendre, and Old French descendere, descendre (“to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.”) (modern French descendre), and from their etymon Latin dēscendere, the present active infinit…

ex: they descended the river in boats
to descend a ladder

ex: The beggar may descend from a prince.

to physically move or pass from a higher to a lower place or position
Synonym of descent (“instance of descending; sloping incline or passage; way down; decline, etc.”).

s.def: Descending; going down.
ex: The elevator resumed its descendant trajectory.
Azure, surmounting a cloud argent, an American eagle descendant, wings endorsed proper, between his beak four lightning streaks, […]

s.def: Descending from a biological ancestor.
ex: Power in the kingdom is transferred in a descendant manner.

s.def: Proceeding from a figurative ancestor or source.
One of the progeny of a specified person, at any distance of time or through any number of generations.
ex: Meronyms: issue, line, progeny; family; clan

a lineal descendant of Charlemagne

ex: Dogs evolved as descendants of early wolves.

s.def: A thing that derives directly from a given precursor or source.
ex: This famous medieval manuscript has many descendants.

s.def: A language that is descended from another.
ex: English and Scots are the descendants of Old English.

s.def: A word or form in one language that is descended from a counterpart in an ancestor language.
ex: The direct descendant of this form is the Slavic aorist: Sb.-Cr. nȍsī, dȍnosī.

s.def: The intersection of the western (setting) horizon and the ecliptic, its ecliptical longitude; the astrological sign it corresponds to.
Alternative spelling of descendant.
Misspelling of descendant.
ex: Traces of the answer, I submit, are to be discerned in all writings by the daughters of Sappho or the descendents of the tenth muse […]

ety: From Middle English and Anglo-Norman descente, from Anglo-Norman descendre (“to descend”); see descend. Compare ascent, ascend. Doublet of desant.

s.def: An instance of descending; act of coming down.
ex: We climbed the mountain with difficulty, but the descent was easier.
To the north the towering scree-strewn slopes of Saddleback begin to draw nearer as we start the abrupt descent towards Keswick.
The next one surrendered his bike, only for that, too, to give him a second flat as he started the descent.

ety: From Middle English descriven, from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībō (“to copy off, transcribe, sketch off, describe in painting or writing”), from dē (“off”) + scrībō (“write”); see scribe and shrive. Displaced native Old English āmearcian.

s.def: To represent in words.
ex: The feeling is difficult to describe, but not unpleasant.

ex: to describe a circle by the compasses; a torch waved about the head in such a way as to describe a circle

ex: The function describes a very complex surface.

s.def: To introduce a new taxon to science by explaining its characteristics and particularly how it differs from other taxa.
ex: The fungus was first described by a botanist.

s.def: To distribute into parts, groups, or classes; to mark off; to class.
ex: Passed through the land, and described it by cities into seven parts in a book.

ety: From Middle English descripcioun, from Old French description and its etymon, Latin dēscrīptiō, noun of action of dēscrībō (“to describe”). Equivalent to describe + -tion.

s.def: A sketch or account of anything in words; a portraiture or representation in language; an enumeration of the essential qualities of a thing or species.
ex: give a verbal description of the events
a realistic description

s.def: The act of describing; a delineation by marks or signs.
A set of characteristics by which someone or something can be recognized.
ex: The zoo had no lions, tigers, or cats of any description.

s.def: A scientific documentation of a taxon for the purpose of introducing it to science.
ex: The type description of the fungus was written by a botanist.

s.def: The act or practice of recording and describing actual language usage in a given speech community, as opposed to prescription, i.e. laying down norms of language usage.
A descriptive linguistic survey.

ety: From Latin dēscriptīvus (“containing a full description”).

s.def: Of, relating to, or providing a description.
Of an adjective, stating an attribute of the associated noun (as heavy in the heavy dictionary).
Describing the structure, grammar, vocabulary and actual use of a language.
Describing and seeking to classify, as opposed to normative or prescriptive.
ex: He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.

s.def: An adjective (or other descriptive word).

ety: From Middle English descrien, descriven in the 14th century already had the dual sense of "to proclaim, announce, make known" and "to see, discern, discover". On the one hand, the Middle English word is a loan Old French descrier (“to proclaim, announce, cry”), from des- + crier (“shout, cry”); in this case, the word is a doublet of decry, which was loaned from the same French source in the 17th century. Alternatively, as suggested by the spelling descriven, the Middle English word may be a con…

s.def: To announce a discovery: to disclose; to reveal.
ex: His Body was found almost naked in the field, for his Purple Robe he had thrown aside, lest it should descry him, unwilling to be found.

s.def: To see, especially from afar; to discover (a distant or obscure object) by the eye; to espy; to discern or detect.
ex: Wee haue descryed vpon our neighbouring / shore, a portlie saile of ships make hitherward.
And now thir way to Earth they had descri’d, / To Paradise first tending, […]
Dimly through the mists they could descry the long arm of the mountains rising on their left.

ety: From de- + stem of consecrate.

s.def: To profane or violate the sacredness or sanctity of something.
ex: Tonight nothing is too sacred, we desecrate and live in sin

s.def: To remove the consecration from someone or something; to deconsecrate.
To change in an inappropriate and destructive manner.
Desecrated.
ex: Here are the very nooks where the unwashed most abound—here are the temples most desecrate.

ety: From de- (“not, do the opposite of, undo”) + sensitize. First attested in the 1900s.

s.def: To reduce or eliminate the sensitivity of (someone) or in (something); to become insensitive.
ex: Working in an Operating Room desensitized me to the sight of blood.

ety: From Middle English desert (“wilderness”), from Old French desert, from Latin dēsertum, past participle of dēserō (“to abandon”). Generally displaced native Old English wēsten. False cognate of Egyptian dšrt.

s.def: barren area
A barren area of land or desolate terrain, especially one with little water or vegetation; a wasteland.
ex: Not thus the land appear'd in ages past, A dreary desert and a gloomy waste.

s.def: Any barren place or situation.
ex: By contrast, the WR route is an economic desert between Newbury and Taunton.
So the question that is commonly asked is, why put a media incubator in a media desert and have it managed by a civil servant?

s.def: Usually of a place: abandoned, deserted, or uninhabited.
ex: They were marooned on a desert island in the Pacific.
He […] went aside privately into a desert place.
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.

s.def: To leave (anything that depends on one's presence to survive, exist, or succeed), especially when contrary to a promise or obligation; to abandon; to forsake.
ex: You can't just drive off and desert me here, in the middle of nowhere.

s.def: To leave one's duty or post, especially to leave a military or naval unit without permission.
ex: Anyone found deserting will be punished.

s.def: That which is deserved or merited; a just punishment or reward.
ex: just deserts
From the highest spire of contentment / my fortune is thrown; / and fear and grief and pain for my deserts / are my hopes, since hope is gone.
Who will believe my verse in time to come, If it were fill'd with your most high deserts?

s.def: Obsolete form of dessert.

ety: From the former sense of desert to mean deserted (“uninhabited”), particularly common on Spanish and Portuguese maps during the Age of Exploration as isla desierta, ilha deserta, and Medieval Latin isla deserta (“uninhabited island”). Now frequently misunderstood as simply desert (“dry, arid location”) and imagined as almost entirely sandy. As an indispensable thing, from the idea of loving something to the point one would want it on a deserted island where it would be used ad infinitum but nev…

s.def: A deserted island, an uninhabited island, especially one in the tropics and (now frequently misunderstood as) a small and almost entirely sandy desert.
ex: What would I take with me to a desert island?
Desert islands cannot harbour treachery, even from the enemy hidden within man himself.

s.def: An island that is completely or mostly a desert, an arid island.
ex: Why are you marooning me on a desert island? It's probably full of guano. Can't I go somewhere nice?

s.def: Describing a thing considered so personally indispensable or beloved that one could never tire of it, used especially for books and music.
ex: My desert-island, all-time, top five most memorable split-ups, in chronological order:[…]
A roast dinner would be my desert island meal and I'd missed Dad's divine crispy King Edwards each Sunday.

s.def: One of various mouselike rodents species inhabiting deserts:
A British or Australian soldier who served in North Africa with the British 7th Armoured Division in 1941-42.
A wandering prospector.

ety: Borrowed from Latin desertor (“deserter”), from desero (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from desert + -er.

s.def: person who leaves a military or naval unit
A person who has physically removed him- or herself from the control or direction of a military or naval unit with the intention of permanently leaving
One who is familiar with the desert climate and environment.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French désertion.

s.def: The act of deserting.

ety: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- + serviō.

s.def: To earn, win.
To be entitled to, as a result of past actions; to be worthy to have.
ex: After playing so well, the team really deserved their win.
After what he did, he deserved to go to prison.
We don't think your article deserves reading.

s.def: To reward, to give in return for service.
ex: Gramercy saide the kynge / & I lyue sir Lambegus I shal deserue hit / And thenne sir Lambegus armed hym / and rode after as fast as he myghte

s.def: To serve; to treat; to benefit.
Worthy of reward or praise; meritorious.
ex: the deserving poor

s.def: Meriting, worthy (reward, punishment etc.)
desert, merit
ex: I here understand that value which every man puts upon his own deservings from the publick

s.def: present participle and gerund of deserve

ety: From Latin dēsiccō (“to dry completely, dry up”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dē- (“completely, to exhaustion”, a prefix) + siccō (“to dry; to drain, exhaust”), from siccus (“dry”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, de- + siccate.

s.def: To remove moisture from; to dry; (sometimes) to dry to an extreme degree.
ex: Transfer the acetone washings to a tared beaker and evaporate to dryness at ambient temperature and pressure. Desiccate and dry to a constant weight.

s.def: To preserve by drying.
ex: The nuts are then passed into a double disc machine, and this travelling at a speed of 3,000 revolutions per minute desiccates the coconut.

s.def: To become dry; to dry up.
Having had moisture removed; dehydrated, desiccated.
ex: How many years have you been here? / […] / Before a desiccate sky left rivers of cracks / in the belly of your red earth?

s.def: A substance which has been desiccated, that is, had its moisture removed.
ex: The Cy dyes are shipped as a desiccate in sealed packs.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French dessiccation, from Late Latin desiccatio, desiccationem, from Latin desicco.

s.def: The state or process of being desiccated.
An act or occurrence of desiccating.
ex: The most important mortality affecting the larval population was most probably caused by the repeated desiccations of the marsh in the summer.

ety: From Latin, from the participle stem of the verb dēsīderāre (“to desire”). The verb is a doublet of desire.

s.def: To miss; to feel the absence of; to long for.
ex: it put him in thought of that missing link of creation’s chain desiderated by the late ingenious Mr Darwin.

s.def: desired, wished or longed for
ex: O Friend of God, know then that London is the desiderate town even of all Earth's cities.

ety: Borrowed from Latin dēsīderātīvus.

s.def: Having or indicating wish or desire.
Of a verb expressing a wish.
A verbal mood expressing the desire to carry out an act, found in languages such as Ancient Greek and Sanskrit; the optative.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dēsīderātum (“something that is desired”), neuter nominative singular of dēsīderātus, the passive past participle of dēsīderāre (“to desire”), from dēsīderō (“to desire, want, wish for”), from de- (intensifying prefix) + possibly sīdus (“star; constellation”) though the connection is unclear. The English word is cognate with French desideratum, Spanish desiderátum. The plural is derived from Latin dēsīderāta.

s.def: Something that is wished for, or considered desirable, particularly when thought to be essential.
ex: The kettle was singing on the side, and a thin white column of smoke announced, that desideratum of tea-makers, that the water boiled at a gallop.
Money is probably a desideratum under almost any circumstance, though it is certainly possible to imagine limitations.

ex: The initial design of the park was rejected for being too expensive.

s.def: A pattern, as an element of a work of art or architecture.
ex: We're working on some new designs for our range of summer shirts

s.def: The composition of a work of art.
Intention or plot.

To be hateful of the truth by design.

The art of designing
ex: Danish furniture design is world-famous.

s.def: To plan and carry out (a picture, work of art, construction etc.).

s.def: A specification of an object or process, referring to requirements to be satisfied and thus conditions to be met for them to solve a problem.
ex: The Wikilambda developers charmingly admit that they are not very experienced in language design.

s.def: To plan (to do something).
ex: The king designed to mount an expedition to the New World.

s.def: To assign, appoint (something to someone); to designate.
ex: He was designed to the study of the law.

s.def: A formal, documented general reusable solution to a design problem in a particular field of expertise.
the application of a defined set of cognitive, strategic and practical processes to develop design concepts

ety: Borrowed from Latin dēsignātus, perfect passive participle of designō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of design.

s.def: Designated; appointed; chosen.
Used after a role title to indicate that the person has been selected but has yet to take up the role.
ex: King designate

s.def: To mark out and make known; to point out; to indicate; to show; to distinguish by marks or description
ex: to designate the boundaries of a country
to designate the rioters who are to be arrested

s.def: To call by a distinctive title; to name.
To indicate or set apart for a purpose or duty — with to or for; to designate an officer for or to the command of a post or station.

ety: From Middle English designacioun, from Latin dēsignātiō, and partly (especially in sense 5) from design + -ation. By surface analysis, designate + -ion.

s.def: An act or instance of designating
That which designates; a distinguishing mark or name; distinctive title; appellation.
ex: Man is the most aggressive animal in the sea (and on the land as well), and all the "man-eater" stories in history will not change this designation.

s.def: Selection and appointment for a purpose or office.
ex: His designation as chief justice was controversial.

s.def: Signification, meaning, for example of a word or phrase.
Purpose, aim, intention.

s.def: A person who designs something, or who designs things as a profession.
A plotter or schemer.
A software tool for designing things.
ex: a font designer
a level designer for a video game

ety: From Old French desirable. Morphologically desire + -able.

s.def: Worthy to be desired; pleasing; agreeable.
ex: This applicant has almost all desirable properties.

s.def: Sexually attractive.
ex: The desirable Miss Moneypenny, M's all-powerful private secretary, gave him an encouraging smile and he walked through the double doors.

s.def: A thing that people want; something that is desirable.
ex: There are plenty of desirables on display in the window.

ety: From Middle English desir, desire (noun) and desiren (verb), from Old French desirer, desirrer, from Latin dēsīderō (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”), apparently from de- + sidus (in the phrase de sidere, "from the stars") in connection with astrological hopes. Compare consider and desiderate. The verb, along with Old Norse derived want (verb), has mostly replaced native will in modern English.

s.def: To want; to wish for earnestly.
ex: I desire to speak with you.
[S]eeing you desire your child to live, / Thanks, but you work against your own desire; […]

s.def: To put a request to (someone); to entreat.
ex: And when they founde no cause of deeth in hym, yet desired they Pilate to kyll him.
Mr. Barrett, however, by fawning and flattery, seemed to be able to make not only Mrs. Churchill but everyone else do what he desired.

s.def: To want emotionally or sexually.
ex: She has desired him since they first met.

s.def: To express a wish for; to entreat; to request.
ex: Then shee said, Did I desire a sonne of my Lord ? did I not say, Doe not deceiue me?
Desire him to go in; trouble him no more.

s.def: To require; to demand; to claim.
ex: A doleful case desires a doleful song.

s.def: To miss; to regret.
ex: She shall be pleasant while she lives, and desired when she dies.

s.def: The feeling of desiring; an eager longing for something.
ex: Too much desire can seriously affect one’s judgement.

s.def: Someone or something wished for.
ex: It is my desire to speak with you.
You’re my heart’s desire.

s.def: Strong attraction, particularly romantic or sexual.
ex: His desire for her kept him awake at night.
Doesn't my body drive you wild with desire?

s.def: Motivation.

der: leave a lot to be desired

s.def: A path that pedestrians or vehicles take informally rather than taking a sidewalk or set route, for example, a well-worn ribbon of dirt cutting across a patch of grass, or a path in the snow.

ety: From Middle English, from Old French desirrous, from desirrer + -ous.

s.def: Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; eager to obtain.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

s.def: To cease to proceed or act; to stop (often with from).
ex: Please desist from telephoning me at this number.

ety: From Middle English deske, desque, from Medieval Latin desca, modified from Old Italian desco, from Latin discus. Doublet of dais, disc, discus, dish, disk, and diskos. See also German Tisch, "table".

s.def: A reading table or lectern to support the book from which the liturgical service is read, differing from the pulpit from which the sermon is preached; also (especially in the United States), a pulpit. Hence, used symbolically for the clerical profession.
A table, frame, or case, in past centuries usually with a sloping top but now usually with a flat top, for the use of writers and readers. It often has a drawer or repository underneath.
ex: She organized her notes neatly on her desk before starting the project.
The desk was cluttered with papers and books, making it hard to concentrate.
He sat at his desk for hours, trying to finish the report.

s.def: A department tasked with a particular topic or focus in certain types of businesses, such as newspapers and financial trading firms.
ex: the city desk, the sports desk
the options desk, the equities desk

s.def: Ellipsis of mixing desk.
ex: Each aux out is connected to an effects unit and the signal is then returned into the desk.

s.def: A station for a string player in an orchestra, consisting of a chair and a music stand, or a row of such stations.
ex: The first four desks of cellos play separate parts, making a lush, Impressionist harmony.

s.def: To shut up, as in a desk; to treasure.
To equip with a desk or desks.
ex: Each row of desked benches was stepped up a step from the other until the top row of desked benches seemed to hit its high ceiling.

s.def: To reject (an article submitted to a newspaper or academic journal etc.) on initial receipt, without reviewing it further.

ety: From desk + top.

s.def: The top surface of a desk.
A desktop computer.
ex: Laptops are often more expensive than desktops.

s.def: The main graphical user interface of an operating system, usually displaying icons, windows and background wallpaper.
ex: I installed a new application and it added its icon to my desktop.
Important menus, such as the root menu or Workspace menu, are "pinnable," which means that you can pin them up and keep them on your desktop […]

s.def: A personal computer, as opposed to computers for business or server purposes.
The wallpaper of this interface.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:desktop.

s.def: A computer of a size designed to be used on a desk or table, as opposed to larger machines, such as mainframes, and smaller machines, such as laptops and palmtops.

ety: From Middle English desolat(e). See Etymology 2 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

s.def: Deserted and devoid of inhabitants.
ex: a desolate isle; a desolate wilderness; a desolate house
I will make Jerusalem […] a den of dragons, and I will make the cities of Judah desolate, without an inhabitant.
And the silvery marish flowers that throng / The desolate creeks and pools among.

s.def: Barren and lifeless.
Made unfit for habitation or use because of neglect, destruction etc.
ex: desolate altars

s.def: Dismal or dreary.
Sad, forlorn and hopeless.
ex: He was left desolate by the early death of his wife.
voice of the poor and desolate

s.def: To deprive of inhabitants.
ex: York was so desolated just before the survey that it is not easy to estimate its ordinary population […]

s.def: To devastate or lay waste somewhere.
ex: Then Moath pointed where a cloud Of Locusts, from the desolated fields Of Syria, wing’d their way.

s.def: To make someone sad, forlorn and hopeless.
ex: It is not altogether uncommon to hear a reader whose heart has been desolated by the poignancy of a narrative complain that the writer is unemotional.
Kumalo stood shocked at the frightening and desolating words.

s.def: To abandon or forsake something.

ety: Inherited from Middle English desolacioun, from Middle French, Old French desolacion f, from Latin dēsōlātiō f.

s.def: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.
The state of being desolated or laid waste
A place or country wasted and forsaken.

ety: From Middle English dispeir, from Anglo-Norman despeir and Old French desperer (from Latin dēspērō, dēspērāre), or desesperer, from des- (“dis-”) + esperer (“hope”). See also desperate. Displaced native Old English ormōdnes (“despair”) and Old English ortrīewan (“to despair”).

s.def: To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of.
ex: I would not despair the greatest design that could be attempted.
I sometimes despair of getting anything quite simple and honest done in this world by the help of men.

s.def: To cause to despair.
ex: Thinking of what I was despairing about despaired me further

s.def: To be hopeless; to have no hope; to give up all hope or expectation.
ex: We despaired even of life.

s.def: Loss of hope; utter hopelessness; complete despondency.
ex: He turned around in despair, aware that he was not going to survive.
My daughter's behavior drives me to despair.

s.def: That which causes despair.
That which is despaired of.

ety: From obsolete Spanish desperado, past participle of desperar, archaic form of desesperar (“to despair”), from Latin disperare (“to despair, to lose hope”), from prefix dis- + sperare (“to hope”). Doublet of desperate.

s.def: A bold outlaw, especially one from southern portions of the Wild West.
ex: Surely this was the face of a desperado.

s.def: A person in desperate circumstances or who is at the point of desperation, such as a down-and-outer, an addict, etc.
ex: The shortstops and desperados were not permitted to play in this marker crap game.

s.def: A person who is desperately in love or is desperate for a romantic or sexual relationship.
A piece that seems determined to give itself up, typically to bring about stalemate or perpetual check.

ety: From Middle English desperat(e) (“desperate”), borrowed from Latin dēspērātus, perfect passive participle of dēspērō (“to be without hope”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun is derived from the adjective or from the Latin source through substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

s.def: In dire need (of something); having a dire need or desire.
ex: I hadn't eaten in two days and was desperate for food.
desperate to eat; desperate for attention

s.def: Being filled with, or in a state of, despair; hopeless.
ex: I was so desperate at one point, I even went to see a loan shark.

s.def: Beyond hope, leaving little reason for hope; causing despair; extremely perilous.
ex: a desperate disease; desperate fortune

s.def: Extremely bad; outrageous, shocking; intolerable.
ex: a desperate offendress against nature
She pictured having a boyfriend over and losing him when he saw her desperate taste in shampoo; however, the chances of that happening were slim.
Whoever's writing the stuff on this has desperate handwriting, like they must be a doctor...

s.def: Intense; extremely intense.
ex: She enraged some country ladies with three times her money, by a sort of desperate perfection which they found in her.

s.def: Involving or employing extreme measures, without regard to danger or safety; reckless due to hopelessness.
ex: In England his flute was not in request; there were no convents; and he was forced to have recourse to a series of desperate expedients.
He dove into the rushing waters in a desperate effort to save her life.

s.def: Desperately.
A person in desperate circumstances or who is at the point of desperation, such as a down-and-outer, addict, etc.

der: desperate times call for desperate meas…

w: desperate times call for desperate measures
ety: This phrase likely originates with a saying of the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates, which appears in his Aphorisms: "For extreme diseases, extreme methods of cure, as to restriction, are most suitable."http://classics.mit.edu/Hippocrates/aphorisms.1.i.html. A similar phrase occurs in Erasmus's Latin adage Malo nodo, malus quærendus cuneus (from his book Adagia (1500), which was first published in English in 1545).http://books.google.com/books?id=VX_Cf4e_66IC&pg=PA73&dq=erasmus+adagia+%22mal…

s.def: In adverse circumstances, actions that might have been rejected under other circumstances may become the best choice.

ety: From Middle English desperacion, desperacioun, desperation, disparacion, disperacion, disperacioun, dispiracioune, dysperacioun, from Middle French desperation and its etymon Latin dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis. By surface analysis, desperate + -ion.

s.def: A state of despair, or utter hopelessness; abandonment of hope.
ex: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation.

s.def: The act of despairing or becoming desperate; a giving up of hope.
ex: in desperation
utter desperation

s.def: Reckless fury.
ex: "The PM’s private reassurances are worthless given her track record of u-turns and her clear desperation to cling to power."

s.def: Ellipsis of bladder desperation.

ety: From Late Latin dēspicābilis, from Latin dēspicor, a variant of dēspiciō (“to despise”), from de (“down”) + speciō (“to look at, behold”). First attested in the 1550s. Equivalent to despise + -able.

s.def: Fit or deserving to be despised; contemptible; mean.
A wretched or wicked person.

ety: From Middle English despisen, from Old French despis-, stem of despire, from Latin dēspicere (“to look down upon, despise, scorn”), from dē (“down”) + speciō (“to look at”). Displaced native Old English forsēon.

s.def: To regard with contempt or scorn.
ex: Near-synonym: hate
Katie despised video games because she saw them as a trashy, boring waste of time.
James still despises his brother for the time he pushed him out of a tree during their childhood.

s.def: To disregard or ignore.

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English despit, dispit, from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). s.def: In spite of, notwithstanding.
ex: Despite being a near-mirror image my of right, my left hand is terrible at these stuff.
Despite all my rage I am still just a rat in a cage.

s.def: Disdain, contemptuous feelings, hatred.
ex: A fals double tunge is more fiers and fell Then Cerberus the cur couching in the kenel of hel; Wherof hereafter, I thinke for to write,

s.def: Action or behaviour displaying such feelings; an outrage, insult.
Evil feeling; malice, spite, annoyance.
ex: And for these Corcyraeans—neither receive them into alliance in our despite, nor be their abettors in crime.

s.def: To vex; to annoy; to offend contemptuously.
ex: to despite his opposites

s.def: despite the fact that, despite [+ gerund], in spite of, although, even though
ex: Despite that I now know that my chest pains are not at all dangerous, if the episode lasts for any amount of time, I start to panic.

ety: From Middle English despoylen, dispoylen, from Old French despoillier ( > French dépouiller), from Latin dēspoliō, dēspoliāre.

s.def: To plunder; to pillage; take spoil from.
ex: a law which restored to them an immense domain of which they had been despoiled
Ripton was familiar with the rod, a monster much despoiled of his terrors by intimacy.
They've come to witness the Beginning. The rebirth of Paradise, despoiled by mankind.

s.def: To violently strip (someone), with indirect object of their possessions etc.; to rob.
ex: A law which restored to them an immense domain of which they had been despoiled.

s.def: To strip (someone) of their clothes; to undress.
Plunder; spoliation.
ex: ’Tis done;—despoil and desolation / O’er Rylstone’s fair domain have blown; […]

ety: From Latin dēspondeō (“give up, abandon”), from dē (“from”) + spondeō (“promise”).

s.def: To give up the will, courage, or spirit; to become dejected, lose heart.
ex: Yet still despond not, but proceed Along the path where fate may lead.
October 16, 1820, Thomas Scott, letter to the Rev. G. Knight, Harwell I should despair, or at least despond.
Others depress their own minds, [and] despond at the first difficulty.

s.def: Despondency.

ety: From Latin dēspondentia, from dēspondēns + -ia. Equivalent to despondent + -ency.

s.def: The loss of hope or confidence; despair or dejection.
ex: Not everyone succumbed to such nostalgia and despondency. Some saw the existential threat to Scots as a call to document what remained.

s.def: A feeling of depression or disheartenment.

ety: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

s.def: A ruler with absolute power; a tyrant.
A title awarded to senior members of the imperial family in the late Byzantine Empire, and claimed by various independent or semi-autonomous rulers in the Balkans (12th to 15th centuries)

ety: From French despotisme; equivalent to despot + -ism.

s.def: Government by a despot or despots: rule by a singular authority, either a single person or a tight-knit group, which rules with absolute power, especially in a cruel and oppressive way.

ety: First attested in 1740; borrowed from Latin dēsquāmātus, perfect passive participle of dēsquāmō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“off”) + squāma (“a scale”) + -ō (“verb-forming suffix”).

s.def: To remove the scales from, to scale; (less narrowly) to peel.
To come off in the form of scales, to scale.
