s.def: A sweet dish or confection served as the last course of a meal.
ex: Trifle is a favourite dessert of the English, but rivalled by pavlova in Australia and New Zealand.

s.def: The last course of a meal, consisting of fruit, sweet confections etc.
ex: I ordered hummus for a starter, a steak as the main course, and chocolate cake for dessert.
Can I see the dessert menu, please?

ety: From dessert + spoon.

s.def: A unit of measure, being equivalent to two teaspoons or two-thirds of a tablespoon, or approximately ten millilitres; a dessertspoonful.
More generally, that volume of a substance which is contained within a dessert spoon.
An item of cutlery; a spoon, larger than a teaspoon and smaller than a tablespoon, used for eating dessert.

ety: From de- + Stalin + -ization.

s.def: The process, begun by Nikita Khrushchev, of discrediting and then reforming the policies of Joseph Stalin.

ety: From Latin dēstinātiō, from dēstinō (“to destine”).

s.def: The place set for the end of a journey or to which something is sent; place or point aimed at.
ex: arrive at your destination

s.def: The act of destining or appointing.
Purpose for which anything is destined; predetermined end, object, or use; ultimate design.
A goal.
ex: This plan will help us reach our destination, victory in the election this fall.

ety: From Middle English destinen, from Old French destiner. Doublet of destinate.

s.def: To preordain.
To assign something (especially finance) for a particular use.
To attribute a particular destination.

ety: From Middle English destine et al., from Old French destinee, from Latin dēstinō (English destine). Displaced Old English wyrd.

s.def: That to which any person or thing is destined; a predetermined or inevitable eventual state; a condition predestined by the Divine or by human will.
ex: Death is the destiny of all mortal men.
And nothing can keep him from me / He is my destiny
Ain't no use to fight it / Don't tamper with my destiny / Any way you slice it / I'm in the hands of fate, you see

s.def: One's eventual fate (not necessarily inevitable or predestined).
ex: Everywhere the atom bombs are dropping / It's the end of all humanity / No more time for last-minute shopping / It's time to face your final destiny

s.def: The fixed order of things; invincible necessity; an irresistible power or agency conceived of as determining the future, whether in general or of an individual.
ex: Dara doesn't believe in using dating apps - she insists that destiny will find her other half.
There were two kinds of beardom opposed here, two futures, two destinies.

ety: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

s.def: Lacking something; devoid.
Lacking money, poor, impoverished; especially, extremely so.
ex: Near-synonym: penniless
May 24, 2018, Alex Vadukul in The New York Times, The Forgotten Entertainer Rag

ety: From Middle English destroyen, from Old French destruire, Vulgar Latin *destrugō, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

s.def: To damage beyond use or repair; to damage (something) to the point that it effectively ceases to exist.
ex: The earthquake destroyed several apartment complexes.
Hooligans destroy unprovoked.
Iesus answered, and said vnto them, Destroy this temple, and in three dayes I will raise it vp.

s.def: To neutralize, undo a property or condition.
ex: Smoking destroys the natural subtlety of the palate.

s.def: To put down or euthanize.
ex: Destroying a rabid dog is required by law.

s.def: To severely disrupt the well-being of (a person); ruin.
ex: Her divorce destroyed her; she had a nervous breakdown and was severely depressed for more than a year.
Other girls in the foster home are eager to destroy her and get her kicked out of the place. It's a tough situation.

s.def: To utterly defeat; to crush.
ex: Remember when Germany destroyed Brazil 7–1 in the World Cup?

s.def: To remove data.
ex: The memory leak happened because we forgot to destroy the temporary lists.

s.def: To exhaust completely and thus recreate or build up.
ex: This exercise is going to destroy all parts of your shoulders.

s.def: To penetrate sexually in an aggressive way.
ex: She got destroyed by her lover on the carpet.

s.def: To sing a song extremely poorly.
ex: JAMES CARTER: The man's destroying a classic!

s.def: To eat food quickly, hungrily or completely.
ex: I could destroy some wings right now.

ety: Inherited from Middle English destroyour, destroyere; By surface analysis, destroy + -er. Designating a warship, it is ellipsis of torpedo-boat destroyer, the longer term appearing at the end of the 19th century and the shorter form early in the 20th.

s.def: That which destroys something.
ex: But it is as a destroyer of grasshoppers that the dickcissel excels.

s.def: A small, fast warship with light gun armament, smaller than a cruiser, but bigger than a frigate.
A larger warship with guided missile armament, usually intended for air defence or anti-ship roles. Often, but not always, larger than a frigate and smaller than a cruiser.

ety: Back-formation from destruction.

s.def: To intentionally cause the destruction of.
To invoke the destructor of.
To self-destruct.

ety: Etymology tree English destruct Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ibilis Old French -ibleder. Middle English -ible English -ible English destructible From destruct + -ible.

s.def: Liable to destruction; capable of being destroyed.

ety: Inherited from Middle English destruccioun, from Old French destrucion, from Latin dēstructiō, dēstructiōnem.

s.def: The act of destroying.
ex: The destruction of the condemned building will take place at noon.

s.def: The results of a destructive event.
ex: Amid the seemingly endless destruction, a single flower bloomed.
If destruction be our lot we must ourselves be its author and finisher. As a nation of freemen we must live through all time or die by suicide.

s.def: A group of feral cats.
ex: A group of wild cats is called a destruction.

ety: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

s.def: Causing destruction; damaging.
ex: The pastures are filled with gay political drop-outs, persons of reasonable intent who found the scene personally destructive.

s.def: Causing breakdown or disassembly.
ex: Catabolism is a destructive metabolism that involves the breakdown of molecules and release of energy.

s.def: Lossy; causing irreversible change.
ex: Blurring an image is a destructive operation, but rotating an image is not.

ety: From Late Middle English desuetude, dissuetude (“discontinuance of a practice, disuse”), from Middle French désuétude (“obsolescence”) (modern French désuétude), from Latin dēsuētūdo (“discontinuance of a practice or a habit, disuse”), from dēsuētus + -tūdō (“suffix forming abstract nouns indicating conditions or states”). Dēsuētus is the perfect passive participle of dēsuēscō (“to make unaccustomed”), from de- (prefix having a reversing or undoing effect) + suēscō (“to become accustomed or use…

s.def: The state when something (for example, a custom or a law) is no longer observed nor practised; disuse, obsolescence.
Chiefly followed by from or of: a cessation of practising or using something.

ety: From Latin dēsultōrius (“hasty, casual, superficial”), from dēsultor (“a circus rider who jumped from one galloping horse to another”), from dēsiliō (“jump down”), from dē (“down”) + saliō (“jump, leap”).

s.def: Jumping, or passing, from one thing or subject to another, without order, planning, or rational connection; lacking logical sequence.
ex: He wandered round, cleaning up in a desultory way.
I teach a class of desultory minds.
subject to desultory fire from the enemy

s.def: Out of course; by the way; not connected with the subject.
ex: Near-synonyms: extraneous, incidental, irrelevant, nongermane, spurious, stray, unconnected, ungermane, unrelated
I made a desultory remark while I was talking to my friend.
She made a desultory attempt at conversation.

s.def: Disappointing in performance or progress.
ex: Near-synonyms: half-assed, halfhearted

s.def: Leaping, skipping or flitting about, generally in a random or unsteady manner.

ety: From Old French destachier, from the same root as attach; compare French détacher and Portuguese and Spanish destacar.

s.def: To take apart from; to take off.
ex: to detach the tag from a newly purchased garment

s.def: To separate for a special object or use.
ex: to detach a ship from a fleet, or a company from a regiment

s.def: To come off something.
ex: Now that the zipper has detached, my winter coat won't keep me very warm.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier, from de- + taillier (“to cut”). Compare typologically Bulgarian подробност (podrobnost), Czech podrobnost, Russian подро́бность (podróbnostʹ) (akin to дроби́ть (drobítʹ)).

s.def: A part small enough to escape casual notice.
ex: Note this fine detail in the lower left corner.
We missed several important details in the contract.
attention to detail

s.def: A part considered trivial enough to ignore.
ex: I don't concern myself with the details of accounting.
Safety at work is not a mere detail.

s.def: To explain in detail.
ex: I'll detail the exact procedure to you later.

s.def: A profusion of details.
ex: This etching is full of fine detail.

s.def: The small parts that can escape casual notice.
ex: Attention to detail was said to be one of the secrets of Gerrard's success as a player.

s.def: A person's name, address and other personal information.
ex: The arresting officer asked the suspect for his details.

s.def: A temporary unit or assignment.
ex: Frequently members of the small police detail dispatched to the scene joined in.

s.def: An individual feature, fact, or other item, considered separately from the whole of which it is a part.
A narrative which relates minute points; an account which dwells on particulars.
A selected portion of a painting.
ex: Shrubbery and the hand of Christ (detail of plate 12)

s.def: Characterized by attention to detail and thoroughness of treatment.
ex: highly detailed
detailed report
detailed explanation

ety: From Old French detenir. Doublet of détente. Cognate with Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, Romanian deține, and Spanish detener.

s.def: To put someone under custody.
To keep something from proceeding or coming to completion; to delay.
To keep someone from proceeding by holding them back or making claims on their attention.
To keep back or from; to withhold.
ex: Detain not the wages of the hireling: […]

s.def: To seize goods for official purposes.

ety: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman detener, from Old French detenir. By surface analysis, detain + -er (action noun suffix). First attested in the 17th century.

s.def: The right to keep a person, or a person's goods or property, against his will; a type of custody.
One who detains.
ex: […] he chatted gaily with his fair detainer, showing no inclination to escape from the bondage in which she sought to retain him.

ety: From Latin detectus, perfect passive participle of detegere (“to uncover or disclose”), from de- + tegere (“to cover”); see tegument, tile, thatch. Sense "to work or solve cases as a detective" a back-formation from detective.

s.def: To discover or notice, especially by careful search, examination, or probing.
ex: The forensic examiners detected tiny traces of the poison on the suspect's gloves.
On entering the room, I immediately detected the smell of gas.

s.def: To work or solve cases as a detective.
ex: Let me introduce myself: Mike MacAdam, hotel detective. / H-how d-’you do? / Mind if I begin detecting?

s.def: Detected.

ety: Etymology tree English detect Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English detectable From detect + -able.

s.def: Able to be detected, noticeable.
ex: There was a detectable pause before he continued. We all noticed it but no one commented.

ety: The adjective is from Classical Latin dētēct-, past participial stem of dētegō (“to detect”), + -ive. By surface analysis, detect + -ive. Noun sense 1 is an ellipsis of detective policeman, detective officer, or a similar construction. The later more general noun sense 2 was derived by extension. The verb is also from the noun. Noun sense 3 (“a work of detective fiction”) is a semantic loan from Dutch detective and Russian детекти́в (detektív), both from English.

s.def: A police officer tasked with collecting evidence and information in order to solve a crime; an investigator.
ex: He worked as a detective with the agency for five years.

s.def: A person employed to find information not otherwise available to the public.
A work of detective fiction.
ex: I very^([sic]) like classic Russian literature. Besides it I read detectives by Chase, newspapers and magazines with news and interesting topics.

s.def: Employed in detecting.
To be or act as or like a detective.
To investigate or find information about (someone or something) as or like a detective.
ex: That sounds like such a super fun game. Wish I'd been there to try it myself or watch you and hear what you were detectiving.

ety: Borrowed from Latin dētēctor. Equals detect + -or (agent noun forming suffix).

s.def: A device capable of registering a specific substance or physical phenomenon, and that optionally sounds an alarm or triggers a warning.
ex: Smoke detectors are mandatory in public buildings.

ety: From French détente, from Latin tendō (“to stretch”).

s.def: That which locks or unlocks a movement; a catch (stopping mechanism), pawl, or dog; especially, in clockwork, the catch which locks and unlocks the wheelwork in striking.
The action of locking or unlocking movement by way of a detent mechanism
Alternative form of détente.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French détente (“loosening, relaxing”), from Latin *dētendita, a feminine singular participle of dētendō (“to relax”), from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from; of’) + tendō (“to stretch”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tend- (“to stretch”)).

s.def: Relaxing of tension, especially between countries; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: Although the Pope [Leo XIII]'s decision was in favour of Spain, it brought about quite a détente between Berlin and Rome.
Analogous structural and political constraints stood in the way of a lasting détente between Germany and Britain.
No step the United States could take anywhere in the world would bring strategic benefits as great as détente with Iran. It has tantalizing potential.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French détention, from Latin detentio, detentionem. Equivalent to detain + -tion.

s.def: A temporary state of custody or confinement.
ex: be stuck in detention
Now, for slacking off in class and for having a serious attitude problem, your punishment is two weeks in detention, with me, starting this afternoon.

s.def: The act of detaining or the state of being detained; hindrance.
The bare physical control without the mental element of intention required for possession.

ety: Borrowed from Latin dēterreō (“deter, discourage”), from de (“from”) + terreō (“to frighten”).

s.def: To prevent something from happening.
To persuade someone not to do something; to discourage.
ex: Their boss deterred them from both taking holidays at the same time, claiming he couldn't manage it all on his own.

s.def: To distract someone from something.
ex: we have in following enquiry, attempted to throw some light upon subjects, from which uncertainty has hitherto deterred the wise

ety: From French détergent, from Latin dētergēns, the present participle of dētergeō, from dē (“off”) + tergeō (“wipe, polish”).

s.def: Any non-soap cleaning agent, especially a synthetic surfactant.
ex: Near-synonym: cleaner (sometimes coordinate)
laundry detergent
liquid detergent

s.def: Synonym of cleansing.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēteriorātus, perfect passive participle of Late Latin dēteriorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from Latin dēterior (“worse”). Cognate with French détériorer.

s.def: To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair.
ex: to deteriorate the mind

s.def: To grow worse; to be impaired in quality; to degenerate.
ex: It was turning into an abysmal afternoon for Newcastle and it deteriorated further when Tiote saw red for his challenge on Jon Ashton.

s.def: Getting worse.

ety: Borrowed from French déterminant, equivalent to determine + -ant.

s.def: A determining factor; an element that determines the nature of something.
ex: The field of the social determinants of health is perhaps the most complex and challenging of all.
The aim of this book has been to assess the determinants of capital punishment without taking a stand for or against the death penalty.

s.def: A scalar that encodes certain characteristics of a given transformation matrix; the unique scalar function over square matrices which is distributive over matrix multiplication, multilinear in the rows and columns, and takes the value 1 for the unit matrix; abbreviated as: det.
A substance that causes a cell to adopt a particular fate.
Something that causes a nuclease to cut at a specified point
Serving to determine or limit; determinative.

ety: From Middle English determinate, determynat, determinat, from Latin dēterminātus, perfect passive participle of dēterminō (“to limit, set bounds”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

s.def: Conclusive; decisive; positive.
Distinct, clearly defined.
ex: Quantity of words and a determinate number of feet.

s.def: Fixed, determined, set, unvarying.
Of growth: ending once a genetically predetermined structure has formed.
Determined or resolved upon.
ex: My determinate voyage.

s.def: Of determined purpose; resolute.
ex: More determinate to do than skilfull how to do.

s.def: A single state of a particular determinable attribute.
To bring to an end; to determine.

ety: From Middle English determinacion, determynacioun, from Old French determinacion, from Latin dēterminātiō. Morphologically determine + -ation.

s.def: The act of determining, or the state of being determined.
ex: the determination of the wavelength of light
the determination of the level of salt in sea water
the determination of the oxygen in the air

s.def: Direction or tendency to a certain end; impulsion.
The quality of mind which reaches definite conclusions; decisive character; resoluteness; fortitude.
ex: Through sheer determination, we managed to escape from the tornado.

s.def: The state of decision; a judicial decision, or ending of controversy.
That which is determined upon; result of deliberation; purpose; conclusion formed; fixed resolution.
ex: The tribunal has reached a determination in respect of this matter.

s.def: A flow, rush, or tendency to a particular part
ex: a determination of blood to the head

s.def: Bringing to an end; termination; limit.
ex: So should that beauty which you hold in lease Find no determination: then you were Yourself again after yourself's decease […]

ety: From Middle French déterminatif. Equivalent to determine + -ative.

A member of a class of words functioning in a noun phrase to identify or distinguish a referent without describing or modifying it.
That determines something.
Sufficient to decide something (such as a question of fact or of law).
ex: When assigning custody, the preference of the child will be considered, but it is not determinative.
An entity does not automatically conclude that any observed transaction price is determinative of fair value.

ety: From Middle English determinen, from Old French determiner, French déterminer, from Latin determināre (“to bound, limit, prescribe, fix, determine”), from de + termināre (“to limit”), from terminus (“bound, limit, end”).

s.def: To set the boundaries or limits of.

ex: The character of the soul is determined by the character of its God.
something divinely beautiful […] that at some time or other might influence or even determine her course of life

s.def: To fix the course of; to impel and direct; with a remoter object preceded by to.
ex: The news of his father's illness determined him to depart immediately.

s.def: To bring to a conclusion, as a question or controversy; to settle authoritative or judicial sentence; to decide.
ex: The court has determined the cause.

s.def: To resolve (to do something); to establish a fixed intention; to cause (something) to come to a conclusion or decision; to lead.
ex: I determined to go home at once.

s.def: To bring to an end, finish; to come to an end, stop, end.

ex: I'm determined to get a good grade on my exam.
Shortly after midnight a determined attempt was made to wreck a portion of Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-on-Avon, by means of an explosive bomb.

s.def: simple past and past participle of determine
A phrase headed by a determiner.

ety: Borrowed from French déterminisme, equivalent to determine + -ism.

The property of having behavior determined only by initial state and input.

ety: Analogous to degrammaticalization, from de- + terminologization.

s.def: The process of a termineme during which it loses its terminological characteristics in a specific domain and becomes the property of general language.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dēterrēns, dēterrentem.

s.def: Serving to deter, preventing something from happening.
Something that deters.
ex: Along with trial by ordeal, hanging was the most effective deterrent that could be devised in an age without police or prisons.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify. Doublet of detestate.

s.def: To dislike (someone or something) intensely; to loathe.
ex: I detest snakes.
Who dares think one thing, and another tell, / My heart detests him as the gates of hell.
Nurse Cramer had a cute nose and a radiant, blooming complexion dotted with fetching sprays of adorable freckles that Yossarian detested.

s.def: To witness against; to denounce; to condemn.
ex: The heresy of Nestorius […] was detested in the Eastern churches.

Something detested.
ex: Neckties are a real detestation for them.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- Middle English trone English throne English dethrone From de- + throne.

s.def: To depose; to forcibly relieve a monarch of the monarchy.
ex: And if it is a despot you would dethrone, see first that his throne erected within you is destroyed.

To remove from any position of high status or power.
ex: “[…] I’m a dethroned elder child, remember. My temper isn’t so damned long as you sometimes think!”

ex: All that was Good and Holy, is dethron’d, / And Lust, and Rapine are for justice own’d.
This injurious explanation dethroned the remainder of Bunson's dignity entirely.
So I am to dethrone my Intellect and set Emotion in its place. Is that it?

ety: First attested in 1729; either borrowed from French détoner or directly from Latin dētonātus, perfect passive participle of dētonō (“to thunder down (strongly); (figuratively, of a person) to thunder, speak threateningly, to rage; to stop thundering”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“off, from”) + tonō (“to thunder”)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂-. The current interlingual meaning seems to be a new formation in postclassical times (to thunder → make a large noise →…

To cause to explode.
ex: The engineers detonated the dynamite and watched the old building collapse.

s.def: To express sudden anger.

ety: From detonate + -or.

s.def: A device used to detonate an explosive device etc.
A small explosive device attached to the railhead to provide an audible warning when a train passes over it.
Any explosive whose action is practically instantaneous.
A gun fired by a percussion cap.

ety: Borrowed from French détour, from détourner (“turn away”).

s.def: A diversion or deviation from one's original route.
ex: On the third day I made a detour westward to avoid the country of the Band-lu, as I did not care to be detained by a meeting with To-jo.

s.def: A temporary alternative route available to motorists away from the usual route due to a closure for repairs, dealing with an accident, or some event rendering the usual route unusable.
To make a detour.
To direct or send on a detour.

s.def: Detoxification, especially of the body from alcohol or addictive drugs.
A detoxification unit.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

s.def: To take away; to withdraw or remove.
To take credit or reputation from; to derogate; to defame or decry.
ex: That calumnious critic […] / Detracting what laboriously we do.

ety: From de- + train.

s.def: To exit from a train; to disembark.
ex: If you plan to detrain at the next stop, please begin gathering your belongings.
As the train came to a halt at the depot, Anne detrained swiftly and ran toward the river.
Lucy, loved by everyone in her family, refused to detrain and insisted on staying aboard for the entire journey.

s.def: To remove (a passenger or passengers) from a train; to evacuate (passengers) from a train.
ex: Following the accident passengers were detrained through the rear cab.

s.def: To reduce one's training, particularly during the offseason, in preparation for a cycle of retraining.
To transfer air from an organized air current to the surrounding atmosphere.

ety: From Old French detriement, from Latin detrimentum (“loss, damage, literally a rubbing off”), from dēterere (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terere (“to rub”). Detriment is related to the word detritus, and built on similar foundations to the word impediment.

s.def: Harm, hurt, damage.
ex: "Would it be fair to say that when it came to making trouble, you'd make up for what you didn't absolutely know . . . and to our detriment?"

s.def: A charge made to students and barristers for incidental repairs of the rooms they occupy.
The position or state of a planet when it is in the sign opposite its house, considered to weaken it.
The position or state of being eclipsed, entirely dark (sable).
ex: Argent, a Moon in her detriment or Eclipse Sable[…]
Moon in its Detriment, or Wane
Argent; a Moon in her detriment, Sable. This word is used in heraldry to denote her being eclipsed.

s.def: To be detrimental to; to harm or mar.

ety: From Medieval Latin *dētrīmentālis, from Latin dētrīmentum (“harm”), from dēterō (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terō (“to rub or grab”).

s.def: Causing damage or harm.
ex: Smoking tobacco can be detrimental to your health.

s.def: attrition; erosion by friction

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dētrītus (“(that which is) rubbed away”), from dēterō (“rub away”).

Organic waste material from decomposing dead plants or animals.
Any debris or fragments of disintegrated material.
Rock consisting of accumulated debris from decayed rocks, like sand, that often is joined by cement.

ety: From French détroit (“strait”) in Rivière du Détroit (Detroit River). Doublet of district, via Latin.

s.def: The largest city and former capital of Michigan, United States, a major port on the Detroit River, known as the traditional automotive center of the U.S. It is the county seat of Wayne County.
The United States' automotive industry.
ex: 'Cause in the real world they're shutting Detroit down / While the boss man takes his bonus pay and jets on out of town.

ety: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dētruncātus, perfect passive participle of dētruncō (“to cut off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + truncō (“to maim, shorten, cut off”).

s.def: To truncate (shorten by cutting, or lop off)

ety: From Middle English dewes (“two”), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French deus, from Latin duo. The word was used by Ford Motor Co. in 1932 to describe a two-seater car model.

s.def: A tied game where either player can win by scoring two consecutive points.
A card with two pips, one of four in a standard deck of playing cards.
The amount of two dollars or two pounds.
ex: Lend me a deuce until next week, will ya?

Douche.
A 1932 Ford.

A side of a die with two spots.
A cast of dice totalling two.
The number two.
ex: Bisexual male, 28, doing a deuce in a segregated housing unit due to positive HIV test result, seeks correspondence from both genders.

ety: From Ancient Greek δευτεραγωνιστής (deuteragōnistḗs, literally “second actor”), originally in Greek drama, from ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”). By surface analysis, deuter- (“second”) + agonist (“combatant, participant”).

s.def: A secondary character; specifically, the second most important character (after the protagonist).
An actor playing a role (potentially all roles) requiring a second actor to be present on the stage, opposite the protagonist.

ety: From deutero- + -ium. Coined by American physical chemist Harold Urey, from Ancient Greek δεύτερος (deúteros, “second”).

s.def: An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron in each atom - 21H.
ex: Heavy water is "heavy" because it contains deuterium.

s.def: An atom of this isotope.
ex: There were about 80 deuteriums for every million protiums, and virtually no tritium.

ety: From deutero- + -gamy, from Ancient Greek. Literally, second wedding or marriage.

s.def: A second marriage, after the death of the first husband or wife; in distinction from bigamy, as defined in the old canon law.
ex: You here see that unfortunate divine, who has so long , and it would ill become me to say , successfully , fought against the deuterogamy of the age

ety: From the name which the book bears in the Septuagint (Ancient Greek Δευτερονόμιον (Deuteronómion), from δεύτερος (deúteros, “second”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”) + -ιον (-ion), and in the Vulgate Latin Deuteronomium). This is based upon the erroneous Septuagint rendering of משנה התורה הזאת (mishneh ha-torah ha-zot) (17:18), which grammatically can mean only "a repetition [that is, a copy] of this law," but which is rendered by the Septuagint τὸ Δευτερονόμιον τοῦτο (tò Deuteronómion toûto), as though…

s.def: The fifth of the Books of Moses in the Old Testament of the Bible, the fifth book in the Torah.

ety: Borrowed from Romanian Deva.

s.def: A city in Hunedoara County, Romania.
To devalue, reduce in value.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English valuation English devaluation From de- + valuation.

s.def: Depreciation.
The removal or lessening of something's value.
ex: According to Braverman's thesis, Taylorism, or scientific management, has been the key feature in the devaluation and dequalification of work.

s.def: The intentional or deliberate lowering of a currency's value compared to another country's currency or a standard value (e.g. the price of gold).

ety: Borrowed from Latin dēvastātus, perfect passive participle of dēvastō (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)); from dē- (augmentative prefix) + vastō (“to destroy, lay waste”). See vast. First attested in 1638.

s.def: To ruin many or all things over a large area, such as most or all buildings of a city, or cities of a region, or trees of a forest.
To destroy a whole collection of related ideas, beliefs, and strongly held opinions.
To break beyond recovery or repair so that the only options are abandonment or the clearing away of useless remains (if any) and starting over.
To greatly demoralize, to cause to suffer intense grief or dismay

ety: Borrowed from French développer, from Middle French desveloper, from Old French desveloper, from des- + voloper, veloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian sviluppare, Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vloppō, *wloppō (“to wrap”) ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrappaną, *wlappaną (“to wrap, roll up, turn, wind”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, bend”) http://www.wordnik.com/words/envelop. Akin to Middle English wlappen (“to wrap, fold”…

s.def: To progress through a sequence of stages.

s.def: To create.
ex: I need to develop a plan for the next three weeks.

s.def: To bring out images latent in photographic film.
ex: Please develop this roll of film.

s.def: To discover, find out; to uncover.
ex: ‘The mystery which I cannot develop, may by that time be removed […].’

s.def: To change with a specific direction, progress.
ex: Let's see how things develop and then make our decision.

s.def: To advance; to further; to promote the growth of.
ex: We must develop our own resources to the utmost.

s.def: To acquire something usually over a period of time.
ex: I have been in England enough to develop a British accent.
You will develop calluses if you play the cello.
She developed bad eating habits.

A district of Bangladesh, where the capital is located in.
A division of Bangladesh, where the district and the capital are located in.

ety: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit धर्म (dhárma, “that which upholds or supports”). The definitions pertaining to Buddhism are influenced by dhamma, a loan word from Pali. Doublet of dhamma and firm.

s.def: The natural order of the universe; natural law, cosmic order.
One's obligation in respect to one's position in society, or the universe; one's duty, societally or cosmically.
The teachings of the Buddha as one's personal path to enlightenment.
The teachings of the Buddha as a practice to be promulgated and taught.
Rule of conduct.
ex: Jain ethical code prescribes two dharmas or rules of conduct.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic ذِكْر (ḏikr).

s.def: A Sufi Islamic prayer whereby a phrase or expression of praise is repeated continually.
ex: When all had eaten and prayed the first night prayer, they began to recite their dhikr, then they began the musical recital.
We prayed together and we practised dhikr, the recitation of the ninety-nine revealed names of God.

ety: Borrowed from Dhivehi ދިވެހި (divehi).

s.def: An Indo-Aryan language, the official language of the Republic of Maldives.

ety: From Arabic ذُو الْحِجَّة (ḏū l-ḥijja), from Arabic ذُو (ḏū, “possessor of”) + Arabic الْحِجَّة (al-ḥijja, “the pilgrimage”).

s.def: The twelfth and final month of the Islamic calendar, during which the hajj takes place.

s.def: A prophet of Islam, sometimes identified with Ezekiel in the Bible.
A given name in Arabic.

ety: From Arabic ذُو الْقَعْدَة (ḏū l-qaʕda).

s.def: The eleventh month of the Islamic calendar.

ety: From Arabic ذُو الْقَرْنَيْن (ḏū l-qarnayn, literally “the one with the two horns”).

s.def: The powerful ruler (traditionally believed to be a reference to Alexander the Great) who built the wall that keeps Gog and Magog from attacking mankind.

ety: From Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr, “noon”), in صَلَاة اَلظُّهْر (ṣalāt aẓ-ẓuhr, “noon prayer”).

ex: Each afternoon – immediately following the dhuhur or midday prayers – he was summoned to Fatima's tent for a question-and-answer period.

ety: From Arabic ذُو النُّون (ḏū n-nūn) + -id.

ety: From French diabase, from Ancient Greek διάβασις (diábasis).

ety: From Latin diabētēs (“siphon”), from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs), from Ancient Greek διαβαίνω (diabaínō, “to pass through”).

s.def: Diabetes mellitus; any of a group of metabolic diseases whereby a person (or other animal) has high blood sugar due to an inability to produce, or inability to metabolize, sufficient quantities of the hormone insulin.
Any food or beverage with a high amount of sugar.
ex: This milkshake is pure diabetes, as my friends and I agreed on as a joke when we first came to Black Tap.

s.def: Diabetes insipidus; any condition characterized by excessive or incontinent urine, now specifically as caused by impaired production of, or response to, the antidiuretic hormone vasopressin.

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).

s.def: A medical disorder commonly called diabetes, characterized by varying or persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels), especially after eating. It is classified in two types, which are different etiologically but similar in clinical effects: type 1 and type 2.
ex: Patients initially may seek medical attention for diabetes mellitus, which becomes clinically manifest a few years after the onset of pancreatalgia.

ety: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).

s.def: To control or select something with a dial, or (figuratively) as if with a dial.
ex: The lead guitarist for the rock band Spinal Tap dialed his amplifier to 11.

s.def: A variety of a language that is characteristic of a particular area, community, or social group, differing from other varieties of the same language in relatively minor ways as regards grammar, phonology, and lexicon.

A lect (often a regional or minority language) as part of a group or family of languages, especially if they are viewed as a single language, or if contrasted with a standardized idiom that is considered the 'true' form of the language (for example, Bavarian as contrasted with Standard German).

s.def: A variant form of the vocalizations of a bird species restricted to a certain area or population.

s.def: To put into dialogue form.

ety: From Middle English difficult (ca. 1400), a back-formation from difficulte (whence modern difficulty), from Old French difficulté, from Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile. ety: From Middle English difficulte, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman difficulte and their etymon Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile and difficult. ety: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

Exchange of airborne media between regions in space in an apparently random motion of a small scale.
The movement of water vapor from regions of high concentration (high water vapor pressure) toward regions of lower concentration.

ety: From Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “terrible, awesome, mighty, fearfully great”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard, reptile”). Coined as Dinosaur(s) and Dinosauria by paleontologist Richard Owen in 1841/1842.

s.def: prehistoric reptile
Those animals of the clade Dinosauria that existed during the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods and are now extinct.
ex: Despite what some cartoons portray, no humans were around when dinosaurs roamed the Earth.

s.def: Any of the animals belonging to the clade Dinosauria, including its sole surviving lineage: Neornithes.
Any extinct reptile, not necessarily belonging to Dinosauria, that existed between about 230 million and 65 million years ago, as well as the stem-mammal Dimetrodon.
ex: Pterosaurs, plesiosaurs, icthyosaurs — I don't know, they're all dinosaurs to me!
"Not a bird, my dear Roxton - not a bird." "A beast?" "No; a reptile - a dinosaur."
‘Dinosaur!’ Denham exploded. ‘By the Power! A dinosaur!’

s.def: Someone or something that is very old or old-fashioned, especially someone who is not willing to change and adapt.
ex: She may be a tough old bird, but it's a mistake to write her off as a dinosaur; you do so at your own risk.
The sign in the window said for sale or trade on the last remaining dinosaur Detroit made.

s.def: Anything no longer in common use or practice.

ety: From Middle English dint, dent, dünt, from Old English dynt (“dint, blow, strike, stroke, bruise, stripe; the mark left by a blow; the sound or noise made by a blow, thud”), from Proto-Germanic *duntiz (“a blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰen- (“to strike, hit”). Cognate with Swedish dialectal dunt, Icelandic dyntr (“a dint”). Doublet of dent.

s.def: Especially in by dint of: force, power.
ex: O, now you weep; and, I perceive, you feel / The dint of pity
It was by dint of passing strength / That he moved the massy stone at length.

s.def: The mark left by a blow; an indentation or impression made by violence; a dent.
ex: His hands had made a dint, and hurt his maid; / Explored her limb by limb, and feared to find / So rude a gripe had left a livid mark behind.
[A]nd read the naked shield, […] Of every dint a sword had beaten in it, / And every scratch a lance had made upon it

s.def: A blow, stroke, especially dealt in a fight.
ex: Much daunted with that dint, her sence was dazd […]

s.def: To dent.
ex: Your helmet was dinted in as if by a great shot.
And, in that moment came one, fierce and wild of aspect, in dinted casque and rusty mail who stood and watched--ah God!

s.def: Pronunciation spelling of didn’t.

ety: From Middle English diocise, from Old French diocese, from Late Latin diocēsis, from Latin dioecēsis (“district under a governor”), from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis, “internal administration”).

s.def: An ecclesiastical territory administered by a bishop.
An administrative division of the later Roman Empire, established by the Herodian tetrarchy.

ety: From Latin Dioclētiānus, Latinate form of Ancient Greek Διοκλῆς (Dioklês). The Roman emperor was named so after his home town of Dioclea in Illyricum.

s.def: Roman cognomen, particularly borne by the Roman emperor Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus (245-313).

ety: From di- (“two”) + -ode. Learned formation, coined by William Henry Eccles in 1919, after Ancient Greek δίοδος (díodos, “passage through”), which however is formed not with δι- (di-, “two”) but with δια- (dia-, “through”).

s.def: An electronic device that allows current to flow in one direction only; used chiefly as a rectifier.
ex: I propose to give the name diode to a tube with two electrodes.
In this circuit when the diode is forward biased, the voltage across the diode remains fairly close to the diode's barrier potential.

ety: From di- + -oecious.

s.def: Having the male and female reproductive organs on separate plants (of the same species) rather than different parts of the same plant.
Having two distinct sexes.

ety: From Latin Diogenēs, from Ancient Greek Διογένης (Diogénēs).

s.def: Ancient Greek name
A transliteration of the Ancient Greek male given name Διογένης (Diogénēs).
Diogenes of Sinope, an Ancient Greek philosopher (c.412-c.323 BC), the most famous of Cynic philosophers.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Dionȳsus, from Ancient Greek Διόνῡσος (Diónūsos).

s.def: The god of wine, ivy and grapes, specifically its intoxication and social influence, but also the patron of agriculture and the theater. Also related to the mystery of religion, as in "spiritual intoxication".
ex: All hail slain and risen God / All hail Dionysus / Come blessed Dionysus, various nam'd, bull-fac'd / Begot from the thunder, Bacchus fam'd

ety: From Latin dioptra, from Ancient Greek διόπτρα (dióptra).

s.def: A unit of measure of the power of a lens or mirror, equal to the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Myopia is diagnosed and measured in diopters.
The dioptre adjustment mechanism of a pair of binoculars or of a camera viewfinder.
A lens element attached to the front of a photographic lens to shorten the lens's minimum focus distance; also called a "close-up filter".
Any lens system, such as a telescope.
A theodolite or similar surveyor’s angle measuring device.
An alidade.
A surgical speculum.
An instrument for drawing the skull by projections.

ety: Borrowed from French diorama.

s.def: A three-dimensional display of a scenery, often having a painted background in front of which models are arranged, e.g. in a museum where stuffed animals are presented against a painted landscape.

ety: From French diorite, invented by mineralogist Alexandre Brongniart (1770-1847), derived from Ancient Greek διορίζω (diorízō, “distinguish”), from δι- plus ὁρίζω (horízō, “to limit”).

s.def: A grey intrusive igneous rock composed mostly of plagioclase feldspar, biotite, hornblende and/or pyroxene.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Hellenic *dwi- Ancient Greek δῐ- (dĭ-)bor. Latin di-bor. English di- Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-der.? Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús) Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁os Proto-Hellenic *génos Ancient Greek γένος (génos) French oxygène Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱéh₁yeti Proto-…

s.def: Any oxide containing two oxygen atoms in each molecule.
ex: Discoid lesions and minor subacute involvement may be controlled by freezing with carbon dioxide or a course of atabrine.
Kruban is a tidally-locked Venusian hothouse, its surface perpetually obscured by clouds of sulfur and carbon dioxides.

ety: PIE word *dwóh₁ From di- (prefix meaning ‘double; two’) + ox(ygen) + -in (suffix indicating a neutral chemical compound), a reference to the fact that the compound has two oxygen atoms.

s.def: Any of a broad range of toxic or carcinogenic halogenated polycyclic compounds that occur as byproducts of herbicides.
The unsaturated six-membered heterocycle having four carbon atoms, two oxygen atoms, and two double bonds (molecular formula C₄H₄O₂); 1,2-dioxin and 1,4-dioxin.
The parent compound dibenzo-1,4-dioxin or dibenzo-p-dioxin (molecular formula C₁₂H₈O₂), in which two benzene rings are connected through two oxygen atoms; dibenzodioxin, oxanthrene.

ety: From Middle English dippen, from Old English dyppan, from Proto-West Germanic *duppjan, from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną; see *daupijaną (“to dip”). Related to deep.

s.def: to lower into a liquid — see also dunk
A lower section of a road or geological feature.
ex: There is a dip in the road ahead.

s.def: Inclination downward; direction below a horizontal line; slope; pitch.
The action of dipping or plunging for a moment into a liquid.
A tank or trough where cattle or sheep are immersed in chemicals to kill parasites.
A dip stick.
A swim, usually a short swim to refresh.
ex: I’m going for a dip before breakfast.

s.def: A pickpocket.
A sauce for dipping.
ex: This onion dip is just scrumptious.

s.def: The angle from horizontal of a planar geologic surface, such as a fault line.

ety: From di- + phase.

s.def: Synonym of biphase.
Synonym of biphase.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Hellenic *dipʰtʰérā? Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra) Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Old French -ie Middle French -ie French -ie French diphthériebor. English diphtheria From French diphtérie (later for a while also spelled diphthérie) in 1857, which was coined in 1855 with the suffix -ie to replace -ite in the previous term diphtérite for the disease because it affects more than one part of the body.…

s.def: A serious infectious disease leading to inflammation of mucous membranes of the upper respiratory tract, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

ety: PIE word *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Hellenic *dwi- Ancient Greek δι- (di-) Ancient Greek φθέγγομαι (phthéngomai) Ancient Greek φθόγγος (phthóngos) Ancient Greek δῐ́φθογγος (dĭ́phthongos)der. Latin diphthongusbor. French diphtongueder. English diphthong From French diphtongue, from Late Latin diphthongus, from Ancient Greek δίφθογγος (díphthongos, “two sounds”), from δίς (dís, “twice”) + φθόγγος (phthóngos, “sound”). Displaced native Old Engl…

s.def: A complex vowel sound that begins with the sound of one vowel and ends with the sound of another vowel, in the same syllable.
A diaphoneme realized as a two-target vowel in some but not necessarily all dialects.
A vowel digraph or ligature.
ex: An improper diphthong has only one of the vowels sounded; as, ea in heat, oa in coal.
The diphthong ae is sounded like ē (§7); that is, it has the sound of ey in they.

ety: From Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”) + ὀδόντος (odóntos) (genitive of ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”)).

s.def: Having two successive sets of teeth (deciduous and permanent), one succeeding the other.
ex: a diphyodont mammal; diphyodont dentition

s.def: Any creature with two successive sets of teeth.

ety: From diplo- + -oid. By surface analysis, di- + -ploid.

s.def: Of a cell, having a pair of each type of chromosome, one of the pair being derived from the ovum and the other from the spermatozoon. Most somatic cells of higher organisms are diploid.
Of an organism, having diploid cells.
Of a certain symmetry class with 24 congruent irregular quadrilateral faces.
A diploid cell.
A diploid organism.
ex: The variation of caryopsis characters in species of Aegilops and wheat diploids is similar to that of wheat tetraploids .

ety: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Latin diplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “folded paper, license”), from διπλόω (diplóō, “to double, fold over”), from διπλόος (diplóos, “double”).

s.def: A document issued by an educational institution testifying that the recipient has earned a degree or has successfully completed a particular course of study.
ex: get a diploma
study for a diploma
hold a further-education diploma

ety: From French diplomatie, a back-formation from diplomatique, ultimately from Latin diploma (“a letter of recommendation or authority”); see diploma.

s.def: The art and practice of conducting international relations by negotiating alliances, treaties, agreements etc., bilaterally or multilaterally, between states and sometimes international organizations, or even between polities with varying status, such as those of monarchs and their princely vassals.
ex: National diplomacy typically deploys its dexterity to secure advantage for one's nation.

s.def: Tact and subtle skill in dealing with people so as to avoid or settle hostility.

ety: From French diplomate, a back-formation from diplomatique (“diplomatic”), ultimately from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “double-folded document”).

s.def: A person, such as an ambassador, who is accredited to represent a government officially in its relations with other governments or international organisations
ex: The French diplomat negotiated the peace treaty.
A career as a diplomat requires cultural awareness and patience.

s.def: Someone who uses skill and tact in dealing with other people.

ety: From diploma + -ate (suffix forming nouns denoting rank or office).

s.def: A professional who has earned a diploma.
ex: You think he could barter and cheat / As vulgar diplomates use, / With the people's heart in his breast?

s.def: To award a diploma to.

ety: From French diplomatique and its etymon New Latin diplōmaticus. By surface analysis, diplomat + -ic.

s.def: Concerning the relationships between the governments of countries.
ex: She spent thirty years working for Canada's diplomatic service.
Albania immediately severed diplomatic relations with Zimbabwe.

s.def: Exhibiting diplomacy; exercising tact or courtesy; using discussion to avoid hard feelings, fights or arguments.
ex: Thoughtful corrections can be diplomatic as well as instructional.

s.def: Describing a publication of a text which follows a single basic manuscript, but with variants in other manuscripts noted in the critical apparatus.
Relating to diplomatics, or the study of old texts; paleographic.
The science of diplomas, or the art of deciphering ancient writings and determining their age, authenticity, etc.; paleography.
ex: In its broadest aspect, the subject-matter of diplomatic is the relation between documents and facts.

s.def: A diplomat's immunity to prosecution and/or litigation under local law.

ety: Probably from Italian or Ecclesiastical Latin diplomatica.

s.def: The science of authenticating, dating, and interpreting old official documents.

ety: Borrowed from French diplomatiste, or from diplomat(ic) + -ist.

s.def: Synonym of diplomat.
A person trained in diplomatics.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ▲ Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *dwís Ancient Greek δῐ́ς (dĭ́s) Ancient Greek -πλόος (-plóos) Ancient Greek δῐπλόος (dĭplóos)der. New Latinder. English diplo- English -opia English diplopia From diplo- + -opia.

s.def: An ophthalmologic condition where one perceives two images for a single object; double vision.
ex: That doctor also noted the diplopia and sent her for a CT scan.

ety: From di- + pole.

s.def: Any molecule or radical that has delocalised positive and negative charges.
Any object (such as a magnet, polar molecule or antenna) that is oppositely charged at two points (or poles).
A dipole antenna.

ety: From Middle English dippere; equivalent to dip + -er.

s.def: A cup-shaped vessel with a long handle, for dipping into and ladling out liquids; a ladle or scoop.
One who, or that which, dips (immerses something, or itself, into a liquid).
ex: A chocolate dipper dips the cream centers into warm chocolate by hand; when taken out the creams are shaped [...]
When the engine runs the dipper dips in the oil once in every revolution of the crankshaft and the oil is splashed on the cylinder walls.

s.def: Any of various small passerine birds of the genus Cinclus that live near fast-flowing streams and feed along the bottom.
The control in a vehicle that switches between high-beam and low-beam (i.e. dips the lights), especially when used to signal other vehicles.
Any snack food intended to be dipped in sauce.
ex: chicken dippers

s.def: Someone who dips chewing tobacco or snuff.
A pickpocket.
A person employed in a tin plate works to coat steel plates in molten tin by dipping them.
A person employed to assist a bather in and out of the sea.
A Baptist or Dunker.
A condiment into which food may be dipped to add flavor or texture.

ety: From dip + -y.

s.def: Lacking common sense.
ex: “He’s dippy,” she informed him. “Absolutely mad. He’ll wreck your ship for you.”

s.def: Having romantic feelings for; excited or enthusiastic about.
ex: “I’ve read in the papers that ye’re dippy about secon’-hand stuff,” she teased, referring to his mania for antiques […]

s.def: Having dips (downward and upward slopes).
ex: "It's not completely flat," Waddicor points out. "It's a bit up and down dippy. The gradients are quite steep compared with traditional lines."

s.def: Involving or suited to dipping.
ex: Also, salad dressing makes a great dippy sauce. Avoid low-fat salad dressings, which are usually loaded with fillers, sugar, and sodium.

s.def: Of an egg: cooked so that the yolk remains runny and can be used for dipping.
ex: The flat was his domain until ten a.m., he informed her brusquely. He liked reading the paper and partaking of a dippy egg in solitude.

ety: From dipso- (“thirst; drinking”) + -mania.

s.def: Addiction to alcohol.
Specifically periodic alcoholism, characterized by bouts of heavy drinking rather than continuous indulgence in alcohol.
A strong craving for something.
ex: "You must regard my passion for painting," he began once more, "as a sort of dipsomania—I really can't help myself."
Such a negative outcome seemed impossible to investors experiencing dot-com dipsomania in late 1999 and early 2000.

ety: From dipso- + -maniac.

s.def: One with a morbid paroxysmal craving for alcohol; an alcoholic.
ex: The dipsomaniac and the abstainer are not only both mistaken, but they both make the same mistake. They both regard wine as a drug and not as a drink.

s.def: A persistently drunken person; a drunkard.

ety: From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι- (di-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “fold, layer”).

s.def: A writing tablet consisting of two leaves of rigid material connected by hinges and shutting together so as to protect the writing within.
A picture or series of pictures painted on two tablets, usually connected by hinges.
A double catalogue, containing in one part the names of living, and in the other of deceased, ecclesiastics and benefactors of a church.
A catalogue of saints.
Artistically-wrought tablets distributed by consuls, etc. of the later Roman Empire to commemorate their tenure of office; hence (transferred sense) a list of magistrates.
A novel published in two volumes forming one continuous story (as opposed to a duology or dilogy).
A literary work consisting of two contrasting parts, such as a narrative telling the same story from two opposing points of view.
Any work made up of two parts treating complementary or contrasting aspects of one general topic.

ety: Borrowed from Latin dīrus (“fearful, ominous”).

s.def: Warning of bad consequences: ill-boding; portentous.
Requiring action to prevent bad consequences: urgent, pressing.
ex: dire need (of)

s.def: Expressing bad consequences: dreadful; dismal.
ex: dire consequences; to be in dire straits

s.def: Bad in quality, awful, terrible.
ex: His dire blunder allowed her to checkmate him with her next move.
And, of course, overlooking 1 ... Q-R8 mate, would be a dire mistake.

s.def: Ferocious and of intimidating appearance, like a dire wolf.

ety: First use appears c. 1817. See cite below. The phrase stems from nautical terminology, where straits refers to narrow, treacherous passages of water between landmasses, posing serious navigation risks.

s.def: A difficult position or situation.
ex: After being shipwrecked on the island, we were in dire straits.
"I understand the country is in dire straits and has a £2 trillion national debt. […]"

ety: Calque from taxonomic name †Canis dirus.

s.def: An extinct canine (†Aenocyon dirus) from the Pleistocene epoch, heavier and slightly larger than the modern grey wolf.
Synonym of warg (“type of wolf”).

ety: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō (“straighten, direct”), from dis- (“asunder, in pieces, apart, in two”) + regō (“make straight, rule”). Compare dress. Doublet of derecho. For the meaning development compare with Russian напра́вить (naprávitʹ, “to direct, to turn, to aim, to level, to point”), отпра́вить (otprávitʹ, “to send, to dispatch, to forward”) connected with пра́вить (právitʹ, “to govern, to rule, to drive, to steer”).

s.def: Proceeding without deviation or interruption.
Straight; not crooked, oblique, or circuitous; leading by the short or shortest way to a point or end.
ex: the most direct route between two buildings

s.def: Straightforward; sincere.
ex: Be even and direct with me.

s.def: Immediate; express; plain; unambiguous.
ex: He nowhere, that I know, says it in direct words.
Nor did the government scruple a direct and avowed interference with elections.

s.def: In the line of descent; not collateral.
ex: a descendant in the direct line

s.def: In the direction of the general planetary motion, or from west to east; in the order of the signs; not retrograde; said of the motion of a celestial body.
Pertaining to, or effected immediately by, action of the people through their votes instead of through one or more representatives or delegates.
ex: direct nomination; direct legislation

s.def: Having a single flight number.
Not employing the law of the excluded middle or argument by contradiction.
Directly.
ex: The walls, which are fixed direct into the ground without a plinth, are made of wattle and plastered with a thin lair of mud or cowdung.
Presumably Mary is to carry messages that she, Anne, is too delicate to convey direct.

s.def: The noun or noun phrase that a verb is directly acting upon.
Such an object when it is in the accusative case, but (generally) not when it is in another case.

ety: From Middle English direccioun, from Old French direccion, from Latin dīrēctiō. Equivalent to direct + -ion.

s.def: A theoretical line (physically or mentally) followed from a point of origin or towards a destination. May be relative (e.g. up, left, outbound, dorsal), geographical (e.g. north), rotational (e.g. clockwise), or with respect to an object or location (e.g. toward Boston).
ex: Keep going in the same direction.

s.def: A general trend for future action.
Guidance, instruction.
ex: The trombonist looked to the bandleader for direction.

s.def: The work of the director in cinema or theater; the skill of directing a film, play etc.
ex: The screenplay was good, but the direction was weak.

s.def: The body of persons who guide or manage a matter; the directorate.
A person's address.
ex: Her aunt Leonella was still at Cordova, and she knew not her direction.

ety: Etymology tree English direct Middle English -ly English -ly English directly From direct + -ly.

s.def: In a direct manner; in a straight line or course.
ex: He drove directly to the office, and didn't stop off at the petrol station.

s.def: In a straightforward way; without anything intervening; not by secondary but by direct means.
ex: I'm sick of asking you to fire him; I'll just do it directly.

s.def: Plainly, without circumlocution or ambiguity; absolutely; in express terms.
ex: I'm going to tell Natalie directly that I love her.
To put it more directly: he's not 'made redundant' but sacked.

s.def: Exactly; just; at the shortest possible distance.
ex: It's directly across the street.

s.def: Straightforwardly; honestly.
ex: He told me directly that he'd cheated on me, and how sorry he was for it.

s.def: Immediately.
Soon; next; in due time; as soon as it becomes convenient.
ex: We'll go to the store directly, but first I need to finish sweeping.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.

s.def: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project, or production (as in a show or film, e.g., film director).
ex: Francis Gurry is director of WIPO.
The easiest way for Neera Tanden to win confirmation as Joe Biden’s budget director is for Democrats to take the Senate in January.

s.def: A member of a board of directors.
ex: [...] the confusion between directors who know nothing and managers who know everything [...].

s.def: A counselor, confessor, or spiritual guide.
That which directs or orientates something.
ex: Installed longer flow director; it now just covers the entire diameter of the 6-in. brine return nozzle, and is 4 in. high […]

s.def: A device that displays graphical information concerning the targets of a weapons system in real time.
The common axis of symmetry of the molecules of a liquid crystal.
A component of a Yagi–Uda antenna.

ety: A calque of French directeur général, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun.

s.def: The highest executive officer within a governmental, statutory, NGO, third sector or not-for-profit institution. In reference to government, the executive officer below the minister of the department.

ety: Etymology tree English director Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English directorship From director + -ship.

s.def: The office of a director.
ex: Near-synonym: directorate (sometimes synonymous)
The corporate bylaws require a quorum of outside directors, so as to balance the directorship.

ety: From Middle English directorie, dyrectorye, from Medieval Latin dīrēctōrium. By surface analysis, direct + -ory. Doublet of directorium. The political sense is a semantic loan from French directoire.

s.def: A structured listing of the names and characteristics of the files on a storage device.
A virtual container in a computer's file system, in which files and other directories may be stored. The files and subdirectories in a directory are usually related.
A list of names, addresses etc, of specific classes of people or organizations, often in alphabetical order or in some classification.
ex: look up an address in the directory

s.def: A form of government with a collegial executive whose members jointly exercise power; the executive of such a government.
Containing directions; instructing; directorial.

ety: Etymology tree English director Late Latin -issader. Old French -essebor. Middle English -esse English -ess English directress From director + -ess.

s.def: A female director.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctrīx. By surface analysis, direct + -trix.

s.def: Female equivalent of director.
A line used to define a curve or surface; especially a line, the distance from which a point on a conic has a constant ratio to that from the focus.

ety: From dire + -ful.

s.def: Fearful, terrible.

ety: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam. Doublet of dirige.

s.def: A mournful poem or piece of music composed or performed as a memorial to a deceased person.
ex: It was as if the night sang dirges with clenched teeth.

s.def: A song or piece of music that is considered too slow, bland or boring.
To sing dirges

ety: From Arabic دِرْهَم (dirham), ultimately from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ). Doublet of dram, drachma, diram, dirhem, and adarme.

s.def: A unit of currency used in the Arab world, currently the name of the currency of Morocco and the United Arab Emirates.
Alternative form of dirhem: a former Turkish unit of weight.

ety: From French dirigeable, from ballon dirigeable (“steerable balloon”).

s.def: A self-propelled airship that can be steered.
steerable

ety: Etymology unknown, apparently from Scots dirk. First attested in 1602 as dork, in the later 17th century as durk. The spelling dirk is due to Johnson's Dictionary of 1755. Early quotations as well as Johnson 1755 suggest that the word is of Scottish Gaelic origin, but no such Gaelic word is known. The Gaelic name for the weapon is biodag. Gaelic duirc is merely an 18th-century adoption of the English word. A possible derivation is from the North Germanic/Scandinavian personal name Dirk (short f…

s.def: A long Scottish dagger with a straight blade.
ex: The Claymore is worn on the left side, the dirk on the right, and the Skean Dhu in the stocking […]

s.def: A ceremonial dagger worn by naval or air force officers in some nations' militaries; formerly, a fighting dagger used by sailors as a boarding weapon.
To stab with a dirk.
ex: Roland Graeme has dirked Adam Woodstock — that is all.” ¶ “Good Heaven!” said the Lady, turning pale as ashes, “is the man slain?”

s.def: To darken.
A penis.
ex: The word dick itself serves as model for two variants which are probably Midwestern, dirk and dork, also meaning "penis"...

s.def: A socially unacceptable person; an oddball.
ex: Near-synonym: dork

ex: With a discreet gesture, she reminded him to mind his manners.
John just doesn't understand that laughing at Mary all day is not very discreet.
Just pass me by, don't even speak / Know the word's "discreet" with part-time lovers

s.def: Not drawing attention, anger or challenge; inconspicuous.

ety: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.

s.def: Separate; distinct; individual; non-continuous.
ex: a government with three discrete divisions

Consisting of or permitting only distinct values drawn from a finite, countable set.

Disjunctive; containing a disjunctive or discretive clause.
ex: "I resign my life, but not my honour" is a discrete proposition.

s.def: Obsolete form of discreet.

ety: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.

s.def: The quality of being discreet.
ex: Bob showed great discretion despite his knowledge of the affair.

s.def: The ability to make wise choices or decisions.
The freedom to make one's own judgements.
ex: I leave that to your discretion.

der: discretion is the better part of valour

ety: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin discrīminātus, perfect passive participle of discrīminō (“to divide, separate, distinguish”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from discrīmen (“a space between, division, separation, distinction”), from discernō (“to divide, separate, distinguish, discern”). ex: Since he was color blind he was unable to discriminate between the blue and green bottles.

s.def: To treat or affect differently, depending on differences in traits.
ex: Low self-esteem can affect both rich and poor people: it doesn't discriminate.

s.def: To set apart as being different; to mark as different; to separate from another by discerning differences; to distinguish.

ex: Nevertheless it is certain, that oisters, and cockles, and mussels, which move not, have no discriminate sex

reverse discrimination

ex: The great discriminations of land are three, and it concerns us to know whether it is poor, or rich, or in a middle state.

s.def: Having or relating to the ability to discriminate between things.

ety: 1656. From Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, dish, disk, and diskos.

ety: From Middle English discussen, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman discusser (French discuter), from Latin discussus, past participle of discutiō (“to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss”), from dis- (“apart”) + quatiō (“to shake”).

ety: From Middle English dogge tothe, calque of Latin dens caninus (“doglike tooth”). Equivalent to dog + tooth.

ex: Dogges teeth, dentes canini.
There are other twaine on each side, commonly called Dogge-teeth.
When he smiled... one of his dogteeth stuck out.

Synonym of houndstooth.
A dogtooth violet.
Alternative form of dog tooth, a jagged leading edge of a wing.

A breezeway, open passageway, or open hallway between two sections of a house.
ex: Old Billy Dill and his ugly wife and son are sitting together in the dogtrot.
The dogtrot was protected from the rain and, because its front and back were open, the Bernoulli principle provided a cooling effect ...

ety: From dog + watch, perhaps a calque of German Hundewache.

ex: […] in the last dog-watch when the drawing near of twilight induced revery […]

The Qatari government.

An old kind of woollen material.

social events
sewage.

ety: From Italian dolce. Doublet of douce, doux, and dulce.

ety: From obsolete doldrum (“slothful or stupid person”) plus the plural suffix -s. Doldrum is possibly derived from dull or Middle English dold (past participle of dullen, dollen (“to make or become blunt or dull; to make or become dull-witted or stupid; to make or become inactive”), from dul, dol, dolle (“not sharp, blunt, dull; not quick-witted, stupid; lethargic, sluggish”); see further at dull), modelled after tantrum.

s.def: Usually preceded by the: a state of apathy or lack of interest; a situation where one feels boredom, ennui, or tedium; a state of listlessness or malaise.
ex: I was in the doldrums yesterday and just didn’t feel inspired.
[T]aken very ill in Cheapside—three pennyworth of brandy, and got home to bed at nine, in the doldrums.

s.def: Usually preceded by the: the state of a sailing ship when it is impeded by calms or light, baffling winds, and is unable to make progress.
ex: [F]rom the bluff-head, where I watched to-day, / I saw her in the doldrums; for the wind / Was light and baffling.

s.def: Usually preceded by the: a part of the ocean near the equator where calms, squalls, and light, baffling winds are common.
plural of doldrum (“slothful or stupid person”)

ety: From Middle English dol, from Old English dāl (“portion, share, division, allotment”), from Proto-Germanic *dailą (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰayl- (“part, watershed”). ex: c. 1650s, John Cleveland, Upon Phillis Walking in a Morning before Sun-rising At her general dole, / Each receives his ancient soul.

Devereux […] was beholden, not only for his fun, but occasionally for his daily bread and even his liberty, to those benovolent^([sic]) doles.

ety: From French dolérite, from Ancient Greek δολερός (dolerós, “deceitful, deceptive”), because it was easily confounded with diorite, + -ite.

Ow! These things are defective. Pipsqueak, be a doll, I need a new pair, pronto!

s.def: The smallest or pet pig in a litter.
A short signal post mounted on a bracket mounted on the main signal post, or on a signal gantry.

A pixel art depiction of a person, typically customized from a base template.
Synonym of doll up.
A temporary barrier used in horse racing.
A miniature house used by children as a toy for recreating domestic settings.
A small, cramped, dwelling-place.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *dalą Proto-West Germanic *dal Old High German tal Middle High German tal German Tal German Talerder. Middle Low German dālerbor. Dutch dalerbor. English dollar Attested since the mid-16th century, from early Dutch daler, daalder, from German Taler, Thaler (“dollar”), earlier Joachimsthaler, literally “of Joachimstal”, the town where the original dollars were minted. The name means “(Saint) Joachim's valley”, from Joachim + Tal. Possibly reinforced by the Dutch lee…

s.def: Official designation for currency in some parts of the world, including Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Hong Kong, and elsewhere. Its symbol is $.
Money generally.
A ringgit, a unit of currency in Malaysia.
Imported from the United States, and paid for in U.S. dollars. (Note: distinguish "dollar wheat", North American farmers' slogan, meaning a market price of one dollar per bushel.)
ex: The restricted purchase of dollar tobacco will, we hope, have the effect of increasing the imports of Turkish and Grecian tobacco
For there are two luxury imports that lead all the others: dollar films and dollar tobacco.

s.def: A unit of reactivity equal to the interval between delayed criticality and prompt criticality.
A quarter of a pound or one crown, historically minted as a coin of approximately the same size and composition as a then-contemporary dollar coin of the United States, and worth slightly more.

ety: From earlier East Anglian dialectal dallop (“patch, tuft (of grass, etc.)”), of unknown origin. Compare dialectal Norwegian dolp (“lump”).

She dollops porridge into a bowl and trickles condensed milk over the top.

ety: From doll + -y, from the given name Dorothy, originally applied either to a woman or female pet or to a children's toy, and expanded to refer to various types of contrivances or devices. The Online Etymology Dictionary, while considering the reason for applying it to such devices unobvious, compares how the names jack, jenny and jimmy are also applied to devices.

Synonym of hand truck (an L-shaped box-moving handcart with handles at one end).
A moving dolly; a small, flat, rectangular platform on wheels, made to be slipped under a piece of furniture or other load.
An unpowered vehicle (trailer) designed for connection to a tractor unit, truck or prime mover vehicle, with strong traction power.
A compact, narrow-gauge locomotive used for moving construction trains, switching, etc.

ety: From Greek ντολμάς (ntolmás) or its etymon, Turkish dolma, from Ottoman Turkish طولمه (dolma), from طولمق (dolmak, “to get full, be filled”). Thus, the word literally means “stuffed thing”.

ety: Apparently from French doliman, dolman (sense 2), ultimately from Ottoman Turkish طولامان, دولامان (dolaman, “robe”), from طولامق (dolamak, “to wrap around”). Compare German Doliman, Dollman; Hungarian dolmány.

He wore his dolman slung over one shoulder and clasped at his throat with a gold chain, and carried his Hussar's bearskin busby under his right arm.
The uniform jacket with several rows of buttons and a horizontal braid across the front originally worn by the Hussars was also called a dolman.

s.def: A woman's garment with wide capelike sleeves.
ex: She turned slowly – she was dressed in tussore and a dolman.

ety: Borrowed from French dolmen. Perhaps incorrectly fabricated from Breton taol maen (taol (“table”) + maen (“stone”)) (the correct compound would be *taolvaen, not **daolmaen). ety: From French dolomite, coined March 1792 by Nicolas de Saussure, named after French mineralogist and engineer Déodat de Dolomieu (1750–1801) who described the stone in 1791 by adding -ite, from place name Dolomieu, Isère.

ety: From Middle English delphyn, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”); the modern form in -ol- is probably influenced by the pronunciation of Middle French dauphin. Compare Swedish delfin. Doublet of dauphin. Displaced native Old English mereswīn (literally “sea pig”), whence English mereswine.

ety: First used as a noun in Early Modern English, from dialectal English dold (“stupid, confused”), from Middle English dold, a variant of dulled, dult (“dulled”), past participle of dullen, dollen (“to make dull, make stupid”), from dull, dul, dwal (“stupid”). More at dull.

Middle English demayne English domain From Middle English demayne, demain (“rule”), from Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”), (French domaine), from Latin dominium (“property, right of ownership”),…

ety: Calque of Arabic قبة الصخرة (qubbat aṣ-ṣaḵra), from صخرة (ṣaḵra, “rock”) + قبة (qubba, “dome”).

ety: From Middle French domestique, from Latin domesticus, from domus (“house, home”).

ety: First attested in 1620; either borrowed from Middle French domestiquer (Modern French domestiquer) or directly from Medieval Latin domesticātus, perfect passive participle of domesticō (“to domesticate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, domestic + -ate.

(intransitive) to adapt to live with humans

To make (more) fit for domestic life.

To amend the elements of a text to fit local culture.

Being the dominant
