ety: From Middle English dormitory, dormytory, dormytorye, borrowed from Latin dormītōrium (“a sleeping-room”), from dormiō (“to sleep”). Doublet of dormitorium and dorter.

s.def: A room containing a number of beds (and often some other furniture and/or utilities) for sleeping, often applied to student and backpacker accommodation of this kind.
A building or part of a building which houses students, soldiers, monks etc. who sleep there and use communal further facilities.
A dormitory town.

ety: From Middle English dormowse, of uncertain origin. Possibly from a dialectal *dor-, from Old Norse dár (“benumbed”) + mous (“mouse”). More at doze, mouse. The word is sometimes conjectured to come from an Anglo-Norman derivative of Old French dormir (“to sleep”) (as *dormouse (“tending to be dormant”), with second element mistaken for mouse), but no such Anglo-Norman term is known to have existed.

s.def: A person who sleeps a great deal, or who falls asleep readily (by analogy with the sound hibernation of the dormouse).
rodent
Any of several species of small, mostly European rodents of the family Gliridae.
ex: Restoration such as this must work around wildlife habitats, and NR came to discover that almost the entire line was a haven for dormice.

ety: From Late Middle English dorsal/dorsale, borrowing from Medieval Latin dorsālis (“of or relating to the back”), from dorsum (“the back”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to dorsum + -al.

s.def: With respect to, or concerning the side in which the backbone is located, or the analogous side of an invertebrate.
Having only one sharp side.
Relating to the surface naturally inferior, as of a leaf.
Relating to the surface naturally superior, as of a creeping hepatic moss.
A hanging, usually of rich stuff, at the back of a throne, altar, etc.
ex: Near-synonyms: altar screen, rood screen (not always different)

s.def: Any of the longitudinal series of plates that encircle the body, excluding the ventral scales.
A sound produced using the dorsum of the tongue.
A fin located on the backs of fish and some marine mammals.

ety: Attested in American English from 1709 C.E.; possibly derived from an indigenous language of the West Indies or Central America, perhaps Miskito.

s.def: A small flat-bottomed boat with pointed or somewhat pointed ends, used for fishing both offshore and on rivers.
ex: From every schooner, dories were being dropped into the shining, clear water. The sound of voices and the splashes of oars carried across the sea.

s.def: Any of several different families of large-eyed, silvery, deep-bodied, laterally compressed, and roughly discoid marine fish.
ex: Pan-fried fish. Barramundi, bream, flounder, garfish, John Dory, snapper and Silver Dory are suitable for this recipe.

s.def: Of a bright yellow or golden color.

A wooden pike or spear about three metres (ten feet) in length with a flat, leaf-shaped iron spearhead and a bronze butt-spike (called a sauroter), which was the main weapon of hoplites in Ancient Greece. It was usually not thrown but rather thrust at opponents with one hand.
ex: The basic weapon of the hoplite was the dory, a wooden-shaft spear six to nine feet long with a metal point at each end.
The principal offensive weapon of the hoplite was his spear (dory). Conquered territory was said to be 'spear-won'.

ety: From Latin Dorylaeum, from Ancient Greek Δορύλαιον (Dorúlaion).

s.def: A former city in central Anatolia, near the city of Eskisehir in present-day Turkey.

ety: From French dosage.

s.def: The administration of a medication etc, in a measured amount; dosing.
The addition of a small measured amount of a substance to something, e.g. sugar to wine.
The measured amount so administered or added (the dose), combined with the frequency of administration and the time period for which it is taken.
ex: Why did he give you only a single 500 mg dose? The correct dosage of this antibiotic is one 500 mg tablet twice a day for 10 days.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French dose, from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), used by Galen and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine, from δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Mostly displaced English drench. Doublet of doos.

s.def: A measured portion of medicine taken at any one time.
ex: Why did he give you only a single 500 mg dose? The correct dosage of this antibiotic is one 500 mg tablet twice a day for 10 days.

s.def: The quantity of an agent (not always active), substance, or radiation administered or experienced at any one time.
Anything disagreeable that must be taken.
A good measure or lengthy experience of something.
ex: a healthy dose of skepticism.
The prospect of becoming a father is a dose of reality that threatens to bring his dream world crashing down.
People who don't get their daily dose of light at the right time of day can end up with worse health.

s.def: A venereal infection.
ex: Don't give a dose to the one you love most. / Give her some marmalade... give her some toast.
It would be very expensive to cure a dose here, as well as unbelievably painful.

s.def: A cold; a common, viral illness of the nasal passage, sometimes with fever.
ex: There's a dose going round.

s.def: To administer a dose (of medicine) to.
ex: "She thought herself broad awake, and I have dosed her with an opiate."

s.def: To prescribe a dose.
To surreptitiously administer a dose of an incapacitating drug (to an unwilling subject); to roofie.
To transmit a venereal disease to.
ex: Sometime back, one of your scarlet sisters dosed me proper.

ety: From doss + -er.

s.def: Someone who dosses, someone known for avoiding work.
A homeless and jobless person.
One who lodges in a doss-house.
A pannier or basket.
ex: To hire a ripper's mare, and buy new dossers.

s.def: A hanging tapestry; a dorsal.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French dossier.

s.def: A collection of papers and/or other sources, containing detailed information about a particular person or subject, together with a synopsis of their content.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁t Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *dʰédʰeh₁ti Proto-Germanic *dōną Proto-West Germanic *dōn Old English dōn Middle English don English do English -st English dost From do + -st.

s.def: second-person singular simple present indicative of do

ety: From Middle English *dot, dotte, from Old English dott (“a dot, point”), from Proto-West Germanic *dott, from Proto-Germanic *duttaz (“wisp”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Dot, Dotte (“a clump”), Dutch dot (“lump, knot, clod”), Low German Dutte (“a plug”), dialectal Swedish dott (“a little heap, bunch, clump”).

s.def: A small, round spot.
ex: a dot of colour
THIS BOOK IS DEDICATED TO A VERY SMALL DOT IN A VERY BIG UNIVERSE

s.def: A punctuation mark used to indicate the end of a sentence or an abbreviated part of a word; a full stop; a period.
ex: The homepage of English Wiktionary is en.wiktionary.org. [read aloud: E-N-dot-wiktionary-dot-org]

s.def: A point used as a diacritical mark above or below various letters of the Latin script, as in Ȧ, Ạ, Ḅ, Ḃ, Ċ.
A symbol used for separating the fractional part of a decimal number from the whole part, for indicating multiplication or a scalar product, or for various other purposes.
In musical notation, a symbol in the form of a small point placed after a note, indicating that its duration is to be augmented by 50%.
One of the two symbols used in Morse code.
ex: The alphabetical signals are made up of combinations of dots and of lines of different lengths.

s.def: A lump or clot.
Anything small and like a speck comparatively; a small portion or specimen.
ex: a dot of a child

s.def: A dot ball.
ex: That left 15 needed from Boult's final set. Two dots were followed by a heave over deep mid-wicket, then came the outrageous moment of fortune.

s.def: buckshot, projectile from a "dotty" or shotgun
ex: Can’t miss no dots Every shot let caused I’m hittin Used to bag it up in the toilet My mumsie thought I was shittin

s.def: A historic speculative bubble based around the Internet, covering roughly 1997–2000.
ex: The excitement about bitcoin and blockchain is sort of like the dot-com bubble—if nobody in 2000 was quite sure what the internet was for.

ety: From Middle English dotage, from doten (“to dote”) + -age; equivalent to dote + -age.

s.def: Decline in judgment and other cognitive functions, associated with aging; senility.
Fondness or attentiveness, especially to an excessive degree.
Foolish utterance(s); drivel.

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English doten, from Middle Low German doten (“to be foolish”) or Middle Dutch doten (“to be silly”). Doublet of doit (Scottish English). The noun in the sense of "imbecile" is derived from Middle English dote (“simpleton”), itself from doten (see above). The noun in the sense of "darling" and "decay" is derived from the modern verb.

s.def: To act in a foolish manner; to be senile.
ex: He survived the use of his reason, grew infatuated, and doted long before he died.
Time has made you dote, and vainly tell / Of arms imagined in your lonely cell.

s.def: To be weakly or foolishly fond of somebody.
ex: Little Bill's parents just keep doting on him.
Jules doted on Chris, spending hours while Chris was at school assembling vast cities out of microscopic Lego pieces to surprise him when he returned.

s.def: To rot, decay.
A darling, a cutie.
ex: But to be sure baby Boardman was as good as gold, a perfect little dote in his new fancy bib.

s.def: An imbecile; a dotard.
ex: How did his death-bed make him a doate!

s.def: Decay in a tree.
Dowry.
To endow, donate.
third-person singular simple present indicative of do

ety: 15th century. From dote (“to be foolish; senile”) + -rel (“pejorative suffix”). The bird is so named as it is easy to catch.

s.def: A small brown-and-black bird of species Charadrius morinellus, of the plover family.
A gullible fool, especially an elderly person with impaired faculties.
ex: This poor dotterel, Sir Arthur, is playing fast and loose with me.

s.def: Any of various small birds of Australasia thought to resemble the Eurasian dotterel.
decayed
ex: some old dotterel trees

ety: From Middle English dottel, dottelle (“a plug or tap of a vessel”), a diminutive of Old English dott (> English dot (“a point”)), equivalent to dot + -le. Related to Old English dyttan (“to stop up, clot”), Dutch dot (“a knot, lump, clod”), Low German Dutte (“a plug”). More at dit.

s.def: A plug or tap of a vessel.
A small rounded lump or mass.
The still burning or wholly burnt tobacco plug in a pipe.
ex: one hand guards the burning dottle of my pipe from the force of the wind
I clenched my pipe in my right fist and poked at the dottle busily with various fingers, first one then another, of my left hand.
He tapped out the dottle on the deck, locked the steering oar in position, and commenced repacking his pipe.

s.def: A baby's dummy, pacifier.
To set pottery flatware horizontally on thimbles.
Stupid or senile.
ex: When days and years proclaim you’re old — A dottle, cripple, gouty fellow, Then for support you can lay hold O’ the upright of your umberella.

s.def: A dotard.

ety: See dote, or compare totty (“unsteady, dizzy”).

s.def: Mildly insane or eccentric; often, senile.
ex: My nan has got dottier and dottier since passing the age of eighty.
"Good God! I don't want another accident here. I should go dotty if I had to face all that again."
JILL: Horses? ... You're really dotty, aren't you? ... What do you mean?

s.def: Having an unsteady gait.
Having many dots.
ex: Look at the dotty pattern on that cheetah's fur.

s.def: A shotgun.
ex: I’m out here from the night till dawn The dotty’s out but I like it sawn

Middle English double English double From Middle English double, from Old French doble, double, from Latin duplus (“twofold”). Doublet of doppio and duple.

s.def: Made up of two matching or complementary elements.
ex: The closet has double doors.

s.def: Of twice the quantity.
ex: Give me a double serving of mashed potatoes.
Britain's population density used to be double that of China.

s.def: A person who resembles and stands in for another person, often for safety purposes
ex: Saddam Hussein was rumored to have many doubles.

s.def: Of a family relationship, related on both the maternal and paternal sides of a family.
ex: He's my double cousin as my mother's sister married my father's brother.

s.def: Designed for two (people, cars, etc.).
ex: a double room
a double garage

s.def: Folded in two; composed of two layers.
Stooping; bent over.
Having two aspects; ambiguous.
ex: a double meaning

s.def: False, deceitful, or hypocritical.
ex: a double life
A fals double tunge is more fiers and fell Then Cerberus the cur couching in the kenel of hel; Wherof hereafter, I thinke for to write,

s.def: Of flowers, having more than the normal number of petals.
A spy who pretends to work for one side, when they are actually working for or passing information to the other.
The largest stringed instrument of the violin family.
The deepest of all male voices.
ex: Voice of a double bass, or simply, a double bass.

s.def: A bed designed for two adults, typically measuring 54 by 75 inches (1.35 by 1.9 meters).
ex: ‘If you sleep on the floor, I’ll sleep on the floor too. But it seems rather a waste of a fine double bed.[’]

s.def: A layer of subcutaneous fat under the chin, giving the appearance of having an extra chin.

ety: From double (“twice, i.e. more than”) + Dutch. For sense 1: Dutch (which historically had a wider meaning) as a foreign language was not easily understood, so anything completely incomprehensible would be double Dutch, i.e. twice as hard as Dutch. Sense 2 expands on this meaning.

s.def: Incomprehensible language or speech.
ex: “Tell him I don’t know what he’s talking about. It’s double Dutch to me.”

s.def: A language game akin to pig Latin.
A game of jump rope with two ropes and frequently two jumpers.
Sex using a condom and the contraceptive pill at the same time.

ety: According to Merriam-Webster and OED, from rare and obsolete French double entendre, which literally meant "double meaning" and was used in the senses of "double understanding" or "ambiguity", but acquired its current suggestive twist after being first used in English in 1673 by John Dryden. From French double (“double”) + entendre (“to understand, to mean”). The phrase has not been used in French for centuries and would be ungrammatical in modern French, therefore making it a pseudo-Gallicism.…

s.def: A phrase that has two meanings, especially where one is innocent and literal, the other risqué, bawdy, or ironic; an innuendo.
ex: Avoid all equivocal expressions, usually denominated double entendre; they are certain proofs of a mean and indelicate mind.
It is not only the teacher's play with single words, phrases, and double entendre that are common in my classroom data.
(There are no double entendres in France, where the phrase does not exist or make sense.)

s.def: A room, especially in a hotel, that is designed for two people and has two single beds (sometimes called a twin room) or one double bed.
The situation where two groups or individuals are the same in pertinent ways, but one is condemned for it while the other is excused.
ex: For example, when discussing relationships, she admitted that she believed in a "reverse double standard".

s.def: A pair of monetary values, i.e. a gold standard and a silver standard, both of which are legal tender.
A double ceremony where two engaged couples, often friends or siblings, arrange for two simultaneous or consecutive weddings.
Closing with a double row of buttons that form a wide overlap.
The action of pushing the button on a mouse twice in quick succession in order to perform a different task that would be performed from a single-click or triple-click.
To push the button on a mouse twice in quick succession in order to perform a different task than would be performed from a single-click or triple-click.

s.def: A frigate with two decks above the waterline.
A vehicle (usually a bus, coach or train) or aircraft with two floors.
Any object with two layers or parts stacked on top of each other.
A headline that is two lines long.

ety: From the notion that if two sides of the same blade are sharp, it cuts both ways. The metaphor may have originated from the Arabic expression سَيْفٌ ذُو حَدَّيْنِ (sayfun ḏū ḥaddayni, “double-edged sword”) or from the Hebrew expression חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (ẖérev pifiyót, “double-mouthed sword”). The metaphor is first attested in English in the 15th century.

s.def: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see double-edged, sword.
A benefit that is also a liability, especially a benefit that carries some significant but not-so-obvious cost or risk.
ex: He added: “Facebook is a double-edged sword. You don’t want to support it, but you have to use it in order to reach a large audience.”

s.def: A neutral principle that has applications that may be either positive (beneficial) or negative (adverse) to one's own interests.
ex: The unintended ambiguity of the phrase was a double-edged sword: it spurred litigation but it also ended up shielding good-faith actors.

s.def: Deceitful; hypocritical; treacherous.
ex: Fame , if not double-faced , is double-mouthed , And with contrary blast proclaims most deed

s.def: Having two functional faces.
ex: a double-faced hammer

ety: From Middle English doublet, a borrowing from Old French doublet, from double, duble, doble + -et. Equivalent to double + -et (diminutive suffix)

s.def: One of two or more different words in a language derived from the same etymological root but having different phonological forms (e.g., toucher and toquer in French or shade and shadow in English). See also Appendix:Glossary#doublet.
A pair of two similar or equal things; couple.
In textual criticism, two different narrative accounts of the same actual event.
An imitation gem made of two pieces of glass or crystal with a layer of color between them.
A word or phrase set a second time by mistake.
A quantum state of a system with a spin of ½, such that there are two allowed values of the spin component, −½ and +½.
A word (or rather, a halfword) consisting of two bytes.
A very small flowering plant, Dimeresia howellii.
A word ladder puzzle.
An arrangement of two lenses for a microscope, designed to correct spherical aberration and chromatic dispersion, thus rendering the image of an object more clear and distinct.

ety: From French doublon, from Spanish doblón, augmentative of doble (“double”), because it was worth twice a pistole.

s.def: A former Spanish gold coin, also used in its American colonies.
Clipping of doubloonie.
Alternative form of dabloon (“fictional currency”).

ety: From Middle English dowbly, doubli, dubli, doubeliche, equivalent to double + -ly.

s.def: In a double manner; with twice the severity or degree.
ex: My mother was always doubly careful when winding the grandfather clock.
Losing a teenmover is doubly painful; so Black continues to make moves.
Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so.

s.def: In two ways
ex: Stealing and then lying about it is doubly wrong.

s.def: with duplicity

To fill with fear; to affright.
To dread, to fear.
ex: Edmond aþelstones broþer · after him was king · / Godmon & doutede · god þoru alle þing ·
Well, all's not well. I doubt some foule play, [...]

ex: There was some doubt as to who the child's real father was.

ex: Ma'am, I have a doubt about today's lecture

s.def: a question (that one has)

ety: From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.

s.def: Subject to, or causing doubt.
Experiencing or showing doubt, skeptical.
Undecided or of uncertain outcome.
Fearsome, dreadful.
Improbable or unlikely.
Suspicious, or of dubious character.
Unclear or unreliable.
ex: The pupils of her great eyes were large in the doubtful lamplight, swallowing their green fires in deep pools of mystery and darkness.

s.def: A doubtful person or thing.

ety: From Middle English douteles, dowteles, equivalent to doubt + -less.

s.def: Characterized by or experiencing no doubt at all, certain; undoubted; undoubting.
ex: There are those who have doubtless faith in revelation.
It is doubtless that the old reprobate who sued for his daughter's hand heard some unsavory truths from the man.

s.def: Free from fear or suspicion.
Without doubt; certainly; definitely; very probably, in all likelihood; doubtlessly.
ex: I cannot remember that I spoke a word, though doubtless I did.
There is also in these matters of Science (though many scientific men would doubtless deny this) a great deal of "Fashion".

ety: From Middle English douce, from Old French dolz, dous, Middle French doux, douce, from Latin dulcis (“sweet”). Doublet of dolce, doux, and dulce.

s.def: Sweet; nice; pleasant.
ex: The sun broke through the cloods, and the douce song o’ a laverock filled me wi’ gledness.

s.def: Serious and quiet; steady, not flighty or casual; sober.
ex: The bookseller, douce man, had seen too many eccentric customers to be shocked by the vehemence of his questioner.

ety: Borrowed from French douche (“shower”), from Italian doccia (“shower”).

s.def: A jet or current of water or vapour directed upon some part of the body to benefit it medicinally; in particular, such a jet directed at the vagina for irrigation.
ex: In the bathroom, they immersed him in a tub of warm water, and then pulled him out and put him under a cold douche.

s.def: Something that produces the jet or current in the previous sense, such as a syringe.
A jet or spray of any liquid.
ex: A douche of spray blinded my brother for a moment. When his eyes were clear of that he saw the monster had passed and was rushing landward.

s.def: Ellipsis of douchebag (“objectionable person”).
ex: You say our records are offensive, (You're a douche, you're a douche.)
I am saying this to you, John Edward. You are a liar, you are a fake, and you are the biggest douche ever.
I said I've got a penchant for smokes and kicking douches in the mouth / Sadly for you my last cigarette's gone out

s.def: To administer a douche to; to shower; to douse
ex: Mrs. McLash's anger was gone completely, douched not nearly so much by the beer as by this attention to her son.

s.def: To use a douche.

ex: The "dough boys" were loaded into army wagons drawn by mules, and with the cavalry at the flanks the relief column started.

s.def: A kind of flour dumpling.
Frybread.

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English doughty (“brave, bold, valiant”), from Old English dohtiġ, dyhtiġ (“competent, good, strong, valiant”), from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg. s.def: Bold; brave, courageous.

s.def: Robust, sturdy; strong and perhaps stout.
ex: Aye, here's a ship of doughty build and strong: But not for lads like you to sail to port.

s.def: Catachresis for dowdy.

ety: Named after David Douglas (1799–1834), Scottish botanist and collector.

ety: From Ancient Greek δυσπρόσιτος (dusprósitos, “hard to get”) + -ium. Compare also unobtainium.

s.def: A metallic chemical element (symbol Dy) with atomic number 66: a rare earth element with a metallic silver lustre. Applications in human affairs include magnets with high performance, which are important in various machines with electric motors.

ety: From dys- + -topia, as if from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía), based on utopia being reinterpreted as eu-topia.

s.def: A miserable, dysfunctional state or society that has a very poor standard of living or severe censorship, oppression, etc.
ex: Recollections tattooed with stiletto reasons and a sorrowful slant of light admitting of dystopiae already petrified in progress.
Like many dystopiae, it ends up with the lead characters wandering into a sylvan wilderness (an English wood) away from the nasty city.

s.def: Anatomical tissue that is not found in its usual place.
ex: The patient suffers from adrenal dystopia.
2. Dystopiæ of separate organs.
While harelips were mostly associated with dystopiae of the incisor teeth, median jaw fusion was accompanied by characteristic dental fusion.

ety: Etymology tree English dystopia Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English dystopian From dystopia + -an.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a dystopia.
ex: The whole city is immersed in a dystopian-looking smog: urban streets in sepia, emptier than usual, bathed in an eerie quiet.

s.def: Dire; characterized by human suffering or misery.

ety: From dys- + -trophy, literally “bad growth”, as in the opposite of growth.

s.def: A wasting of body tissues, of either genetic origin or due to inadequate or defective nutrition.

ety: From Turkic languages (compare Nogai йигит (yigit), Tatar егет (yeget, “young male”)), via Russian джиги́т (džigít).

s.def: A skilled horseman in the Caucasus and Central Asia.
A brave man in general.

ety: Borrowed from Mongolian зуд (zud)/ᠵᠤᠳ (ǰud).

s.def: An ecological crisis in the steppe-land of Mongolia and Central Asia causing loss of livestock, for example a drought, or a severe winter in which snow or ice block animals' access to the grass.
ex: But the country [Mongolia] is currently experiencing a "dzud" – when a summer drought followed by a severe winter decimates the grazing areas.
